name: Application Security for Web and LLM Apps
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Engineers and architects who build and run web products and AI features and must keep them secure without a dedicated security team.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of find-the-vulnerability, choose-the-control, read-the-config and incident questions.

domains.name: Threat modelling and secure design
domains.summary: Thinking like an attacker before writing code: data-flow diagrams, trust boundaries and STRIDE, secure defaults and least privilege, OWASP ASVS levels for a small team, security logging and alerting, and scanning in the delivery flow without drowning in noise.

domains.name: Authentication and sessions
domains.summary: Proving who the user is and keeping them signed in safely: passwords per NIST SP 800-63B-4, passkeys and MFA, recovery, cookie-based sessions, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with PKCE, and validating and revoking JWTs.

domains.name: Authorization and data protection
domains.summary: Deciding what each user may do and protecting the data they touch: IDOR and tenant isolation, RBAC, ABAC and relationship-based models, Postgres row-level security, encryption and key management, secrets handling and privacy engineering.

domains.name: Injection and browser security
domains.summary: Stopping untrusted input from becoming code or requests: SQL, NoSQL and command injection, XSS and output encoding, Content Security Policy, CSRF, CORS and clickjacking, plus SSRF, path traversal, deserialisation and file uploads.

domains.name: LLM and agent application security
domains.summary: Securing features built on LLMs and agents: the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, direct and indirect prompt injection and the architectural mitigations that work, data leakage, insecure output handling, and permissions for RAG, tools and MCP servers.

domains.name: Supply chain, infrastructure and incident response
domains.summary: Keeping the code you ship and the platform you run on trustworthy, and recovering when something goes wrong: dependency risk, SLSA and provenance, pinned CI actions, cloud and container hardening, security headers and TLS, and incident response.

scenarios.title: Reviewing a pull request for security bugs
scenarios.description: A teammate opens a pull request that adds an endpoint, a query and some rendered user content. Find the injection, access-control and output-handling bugs before it merges, and pick the simplest fix for each.

scenarios.title: Designing authentication and authorization for a SaaS
scenarios.description: A small team is building a multi-tenant SaaS. Choose password, passkey and OAuth/OIDC flows, set up secure sessions, and enforce tenant isolation and roles in one place, down to the database.

scenarios.title: Shipping an LLM feature that reads user documents
scenarios.description: An assistant answers questions over customers' uploaded documents and can call tools. Contain indirect prompt injection, enforce document permissions at retrieval time, and handle model output safely.

scenarios.title: Responding to a leaked secret
scenarios.description: A cloud key turns up in a public commit or a build log. Contain it, rotate it, check for misuse, decide who must be notified, and fix the process so it does not happen again.

scenarios.title: Preparing for a customer security questionnaire
scenarios.description: An enterprise prospect sends a security questionnaire. Answer honestly about threat modelling, ASVS coverage, encryption, logging, supply-chain controls and incident response, and close the gaps that matter.

lessons.title: Threat modelling a small product
lessons.summary: Draw the system as a data-flow diagram, mark the trust boundaries, walk STRIDE over every element that crosses one, and rank what you find by likelihood and impact.

sections.heading: The four questions
sections.body:
Threat modelling does not need a week-long workshop. The OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet frames it as four questions:

1. **What are we working on?** Model the system.
2. **What can go wrong?** Identify and rank threats.
3. **What are we going to do about it?** Choose a response for each threat.
4. **Did we do a good enough job?** Review the model with everyone who has a stake in it, not only developers or the security team.

For a small team, an hour around a whiteboard when a feature changes how data moves is worth more than a big document written once and never updated. Keep the model current as the system changes.

sections.heading: Data-flow diagrams and trust boundaries
sections.body:
A data-flow diagram (DFD) is the most common way to answer "what are we working on". It has five kinds of element:

| Element | Example in a small SaaS |
|---|---|
| External entity | Browser user, payment provider, email service |
| Process | API server, background worker |
| Data store | Postgres, object storage, Redis |
| Data flow | HTTPS request, webhook, queue message |
| Trust boundary | Internet to API, API to database, your code to a third-party SDK |

A **trust boundary** is any line where data or control passes between parties with different levels of trust. Every flow that crosses a boundary is a place where input must be authenticated, validated and authorised. Inbound webhooks, file uploads, admin tools and "internal" services that accept requests from anywhere on the network are the boundaries teams most often forget.

sections.heading: STRIDE as a prompt list
sections.body:
STRIDE gives six categories to walk over every element and boundary crossing. Each one is the opposite of a security property:

| Threat | Property violated | Small-product example |
|---|---|---|
| **S**poofing | Authentication | Forged webhook claims to come from the payment provider |
| **T**ampering | Integrity | Client edits the price field in a checkout request |
| **R**epudiation | Accounting (non-repudiation) | Admin deletes records and there is no audit trail |
| **I**nformation disclosure | Confidentiality | Invoice endpoint returns another tenant's invoice |
| **D**enial of service | Availability | Unbounded export job exhausts the database |
| **E**levation of privilege | Authorisation | Normal user calls an admin-only route |

Record which component, flow or boundary each threat affects. STRIDE is a brainstorming aid, not a checklist that proves completeness; the cheat sheet points to LINDDUN for privacy threats that STRIDE does not fully cover.

sections.heading: Ranking and responding
sections.body:
The cheat sheet says ranking should in theory be the product of **likelihood and impact**: a threat that is likely and damaging comes before one that is unlikely and moderate. Both are hard to estimate precisely, and the product ignores the work needed to fix a problem, so a coarse high/medium/low grid is a practical choice and some practitioners also weigh the effort of the fix.

Every threat needs a response:

- **Mitigate**: take action to reduce the likelihood that the threat materialises.
- **Eliminate**: remove the feature or component.
- **Transfer**: move responsibility to another party by contract; this does not reduce the harm itself.
- **Accept**: keep the risk when no other option fits the business constraints; document why and who owns it.

Turn agreed mitigations into concrete security requirements and tickets so they are actually built.

sections.heading: Worked anchor: middleware-only authorisation
sections.body:
CVE-2025-29927 was an authorisation bypass in Next.js middleware: an internal `x-middleware-subrequest` header could be abused so that middleware was skipped. Self-hosted deployments using `next start` or standalone output were affected; Vercel-hosted deployments were not. Vercel's postmortem advises against relying on middleware as the only route protection. Apps that enforced authorisation **only** in middleware were exposed.

In DFD terms, the team had drawn a single check at the edge and trusted everything behind it. The design lesson is to enforce authorisation close to the data: re-check in the route handler or data-access layer as well as at the edge, and patch the framework. One control at one boundary is a single point of failure.

keyPoints: Use the four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what will we do, did we do a good enough job.
A DFD shows external entities, processes, data stores, data flows and trust boundaries.
Every flow that crosses a trust boundary needs authentication, validation and authorisation.
STRIDE maps to authentication, integrity, accounting (non-repudiation), confidentiality, availability and authorisation.
Rank by likelihood times impact; respond with mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept.
Never enforce authorisation in a single edge layer such as middleware only.

gotchas.trap: Treating "internal" services and inbound webhooks as trusted because they are not the public UI.
gotchas.correct: Any flow that crosses a trust boundary is untrusted input; authenticate the sender and validate the payload.

gotchas.trap: Fixing the scariest-sounding threat first.
gotchas.correct: Rank by likelihood and impact; an easy-to-exploit data exposure usually beats an exotic, unlikely attack.

gotchas.trap: Transferring a risk (for example by contract) and calling it mitigated.
gotchas.correct: Transfer does not reduce likelihood or harm; document who owns the remaining controls and residual risk.

lessons.lab: Pick one feature of a product you know, such as file upload or invoicing. Draw its DFD with every trust boundary, walk STRIDE over each boundary crossing, write at least six threats, score each high/medium/low for likelihood and impact, and turn the top three into tickets with a named response.

lessons.title: Secure defaults, least privilege and ASVS
lessons.summary: Make the safe path the default in the app, the database and the cloud account, and use OWASP ASVS 5.0 levels to decide which requirements a small team tackles first.

sections.heading: Secure by default
sections.body:
A secure default means a new route, table, bucket or role starts closed and someone has to open it on purpose. CISA's Secure by Design work pushes vendors to ship products that are secure out of the box rather than relying on customers to harden them.

In application code that means:

- **Deny by default**: the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet says an application should be configured to deny access by default, so routes require authentication and an explicit permission unless marked public. Forgetting an annotation should fail closed, not open.
- Safe framework defaults left on: output encoding, CSRF protection, secure cookie attributes.
- Debug pages, sample accounts and verbose errors off in production. Security Misconfiguration is **A02:2025** in the OWASP Top 10.

sections.heading: Least privilege in the database
sections.body:
The application should connect as a dedicated role that has only the privileges it needs (`GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE` on its own tables), never as a superuser or the table owner.

This matters doubly with Postgres row-level security. Per the PostgreSQL docs:

- With RLS enabled and no policy, access is **default deny**.
- **Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS and, normally, table owners bypass RLS.**
- `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` makes the owner subject to policies, but superusers still bypass them.

A team that writes perfect tenant policies but connects as the owner gets no isolation at all. Use separate roles for migrations (owner) and runtime (restricted).

sections.heading: Least privilege in the cloud
sections.body:
The AWS IAM best-practices page gives a pattern that applies to any cloud:

- Humans sign in through federation and get **temporary credentials**; workloads use **IAM roles**, not long-lived access keys.
- Require MFA, and do not use the root user for everyday work.
- Start from managed policies and move toward **least-privilege** policies; IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from actual access activity.
- Regularly remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials, and use conditions and permission boundaries as guardrails.

For instance metadata, the OWASP SSRF cheat sheet advises migrating to IMDSv2 and disabling IMDSv1, so an SSRF bug cannot trivially read role credentials.

sections.heading: OWASP ASVS 5.0 for a small team
sections.body:
The **Application Security Verification Standard** turns "be secure" into testable requirements. Version **5.0.0** (30 May 2025) is the latest stable release:

- 17 chapters and 345 requirements, with new material on self-contained tokens, OAuth and OIDC, and WebRTC.
- **Level 1** (70 requirements, about 20%) was redefined around first-layer defences, to lower the barrier to adoption.
- Levels 2 and 3 add progressively more depth for higher-risk applications. ASVS 5.0 encourages organisations to choose the level that fits their risk and maturity rather than a mandated one.
- Identifiers changed from 4.0.3: even requirements that were not substantively modified have new numbers because of reordering. Cite requirements as `v5.0.0-1.2.5` style, with the version, because identifiers change between versions.

What to do first: adopt L1 as the definition of done for every app, pick the L2 chapters that match your real risks (authentication, access control, data protection), and feed threats from your threat model into the same backlog.

keyPoints: New routes, tables, buckets and roles should start closed; forgetting a setting must fail closed.
The app connects as a non-owner, non-superuser role; owners and superusers bypass Postgres RLS.
Workloads use roles and temporary credentials, not long-lived access keys.
ASVS 5.0.0 is current: 17 chapters, 345 requirements, 70 at Level 1.
Small teams: meet L1 everywhere first, then L2 for apps with sensitive data.
Write ASVS IDs with the version prefix; 4.x numbers do not map to 5.0.

gotchas.trap: Enabling RLS and testing it while connected as the table owner or a superuser.
gotchas.correct: Owners and superusers bypass RLS; test as the restricted runtime role, or FORCE RLS for the owner.

gotchas.trap: Rotating an admin access key every month and calling it least privilege.
gotchas.correct: Rotation does not shrink permissions; use a role with temporary credentials and a scoped policy.

gotchas.trap: Starting with ASVS Level 3 for every app.
gotchas.correct: Level 1 first for everything; Level 2 where data is sensitive; Level 3 only where the risk justifies the extra depth.

lessons.lab: In a scratch Postgres, create a tenant table with RLS and a policy. Query it as the owner and note that all rows return. Create a NOLOGIN app role with only SELECT, SET ROLE to it, and confirm the policy now filters rows. Then list the ASVS 5.0 Level 1 requirements for authentication and mark which ones your app already meets.

lessons.title: Security logging and the delivery flow
lessons.summary: Log the events that reveal abuse, keep secrets and sensitive data out of logs, alert on what matters, and add review, SAST, dependency and secret scanning to delivery without drowning in noise.

sections.heading: What to log
sections.body:
The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists the events that matter for security. Always log:

- Authentication successes and failures (failures are early warnings of brute force, credential stuffing and password spraying).
- Authorisation (access-control) failures.
- Input validation failures and session management failures, such as a tampered session cookie or a suspicious JWT validation failure.
- Administrative and other high-risk actions: permission changes, data exports, key changes.

Each event needs when, where, who (user or service and source address) and what (action, object, outcome), plus an interaction or request ID so related events can be correlated. Do not exclude "known" sources such as monitoring tools or internal systems; flag them instead.

sections.heading: What never to log
sections.body:
The cheat sheet says the following should not be recorded directly, but removed, masked, hashed or encrypted:

- Authentication passwords, access tokens and **session identifiers** (hash the session ID if you need to correlate).
- Database connection strings, encryption keys and other primary secrets.
- Payment card and bank data, and sensitive personal data such as health records or government IDs.
- Application source code, and data above the logging system's classification.

For LLM features, do not log full prompts or completions that may contain personal data; log metadata (user, model, token counts, tool calls) and a redacted or sampled form instead.

Logs are also an attack surface. Sanitise CR, LF and delimiter characters, and prefer structured (JSON) logging with a correct encoder: parameterised messages alone do not stop CR/LF log injection.

sections.heading: From logs to alerts
sections.body:
In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A09 was renamed **Security Logging & Alerting Failures** to emphasise the alerting needed to act on logged events; OWASP notes that great logging with no alerting is of minimal value.

- Alert on patterns, not single events: many failed logins across many accounts from a set of sources, a spike in authorisation failures from one user, an unusual bulk export.
- Route alerts to a person on call with a runbook, and tune thresholds so alerts stay rare and actionable.
- Protect log integrity and restrict who can read logs or change logging configuration.

sections.heading: Security in the delivery flow
sections.body:
A small team can add security to its pull-request flow in a few steps, each with GitHub as the example:

- **Code review** with a security lens on changes that touch authentication, authorisation, input parsing, secrets or a new trust boundary.
- **SAST** via code scanning (for example CodeQL), which annotates new alerts on the lines a pull request changes and, by default, fails the check for high, critical or error severity findings.
- **Dependency scanning** with Dependabot alerts and updates. Version updates have a default cooldown of 3 days, which the `cooldown` option can tune, so freshly published (possibly malicious) releases are not pulled in instantly.
- **Secret scanning** with **push protection**, which blocks a commit containing a recognised secret. Push protection is on by default for users pushing to public repositories; for organisation repositories it needs GitHub Secret Protection and is off until an admin enables it.

If a secret does leak, GitHub's guidance is to **rotate the affected credential immediately**. Rewriting Git history is often unnecessary once the credential is revoked.

sections.heading: Not drowning in noise
sections.body:
Turning every scanner on at once on a legacy repository produces hundreds of findings and teaches people to ignore them. Instead:

1. Take a **baseline**: triage existing alerts once, dismiss false positives with a reason, and ticket the real ones.
2. **Gate only on new, high-severity findings** introduced by the pull request, so the build stays green for unrelated work.
3. Burn down the backlog on a schedule, highest risk first.
4. Watch bypasses: a push-protection bypass marked "I'll fix it later" leaves an open alert, while "used in tests" or "false positive" closes it, so review those reasons.

keyPoints: Always log authentication successes and failures, authorisation failures, validation failures and admin actions.
Never log passwords, tokens, session IDs, keys, connection strings or card data; mask or hash instead.
Sanitise CR/LF and use structured logging to prevent log injection.
A09:2025 is Security Logging & Alerting Failures: alert on abuse patterns and route to on-call.
Leaked secret: rotate it immediately; history rewriting is often unnecessary after revocation.
Baseline existing findings and gate pull requests only on new high-severity ones.

gotchas.trap: Logging the full Authorization header or session cookie to make debugging easier.
gotchas.correct: Tokens and session IDs must not be logged; log a hash or a request ID instead.

gotchas.trap: Force-pushing to scrub a leaked key from history and considering the incident closed.
gotchas.correct: Revoke and rotate the credential first; once revoked, rewriting history is often unnecessary.

gotchas.trap: Blocking every merge until a legacy repository has zero SAST alerts.
gotchas.correct: Baseline and triage existing alerts, then gate only on new high-severity findings.

lessons.lab: Take one service and list ten log lines it emits. Mark any that contain a token, session ID, password or personal data and rewrite them. Then enable code scanning, Dependabot alerts and push protection on a test repository, commit a fake test credential, and note what push protection does and which bypass reason leaves an open alert.

lessons.title: Passwords done right with NIST SP 800-63B-4
lessons.summary: What the final NIST SP 800-63B-4 actually requires for passwords, how to store them with Argon2id, and how to throttle guessing without locking everyone out.

sections.heading: Why the old rules were dropped
sections.body:
NIST SP 800-63B-4 was finalised in July 2025 and supersedes rev 3. It replaces the familiar "8 characters, one uppercase, one symbol, change every 90 days" policy with rules built on evidence about how people actually choose passwords.

| Rule | 800-63B-4 |
|---|---|
| Minimum length, password as the only factor | **15** characters (SHALL) |
| Minimum length, password used only inside MFA | 8 characters |
| Maximum length | SHOULD allow at least 64 |
| Composition rules (mix of character types) | **SHALL NOT** be imposed |
| Periodic forced change | SHALL NOT be required. Force a change only on evidence of compromise |
| Hints and security questions | SHALL NOT be used |
| Truncation | SHALL verify the entire password |

Length beats complexity. A 15-character all-lowercase password is about 70.5 bits if it is chosen at random, while 8 random printable ASCII characters give about 52.6 bits. Composition rules mostly push people toward predictable patterns such as `Password1!`.

sections.heading: Blocklists and user experience
sections.body:
The verifier SHALL compare the **whole** password against a blocklist of breached passwords, dictionary words and context-specific words (the service name, the username). When it rejects a password, it SHALL tell the user why, so they can pick a better one.

Make password managers work: autofill SHALL be allowed, paste SHOULD be allowed, and a "show password" option SHOULD be offered. Accept Unicode, count each code point as one character, and NFC-normalise the string before hashing so the same password always hashes the same way.

sections.heading: Storing passwords
sections.body:
NIST requires a salt of at least 32 bits and a hash with a cost factor as high as is practical. Store which scheme and cost were used, so you can upgrade later. It also recommends a **pepper**: a keyed hashing step whose secret is stored separately from the password hashes, for example in a hardware security module (HSM), trusted execution environment (TEE) or TPM.

The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives concrete settings:

- **Argon2id** (first choice): at least m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1, or an equivalent trade-off such as m=46 MiB, t=1.
- **scrypt**: N=2^17, r=8, p=1.
- **bcrypt**: work factor 10 or more, for legacy systems only. It has a **72-byte input limit**.
- **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256**: 600,000 iterations, when FIPS compliance is required.

Do not pre-hash with plain SHA-512 before bcrypt. If you have to pre-hash, use HMAC-SHA-384 with a pepper. Upgrade old hashes when the user next logs in successfully.

sections.heading: Throttling guessing
sections.body: 800-63B-4 says the verifier SHALL limit consecutive failed attempts on one authenticator to **no more than 100**. That is an upper bound, not a target. In practice, combine per-account throttling (growing delays) with per-IP and global rate limits, so a credential-stuffing run across many accounts also gets slowed down. Permanent lockout after a few failures turns throttling into a denial-of-service tool, because anyone can lock out a known username.

keyPoints: A password that is the only factor must be at least 15 characters. Inside MFA, 8 is the minimum.
Composition rules and periodic forced changes SHALL NOT be imposed. Force a change only on evidence of compromise.
Check every new password against a breached-password and context blocklist, and tell the user why it was rejected.
Hash with Argon2id (at least 19 MiB, t=2, p=1) and a per-user salt, and keep any pepper outside the database.
Limit consecutive failures to at most 100 per account, and add IP and global rate limits.

gotchas.trap: NIST still says 8 characters is the minimum for passwords.
gotchas.correct: In 800-63B-4, 8 is only for passwords used as part of MFA. A single-factor password needs at least 15.

gotchas.trap: bcrypt is the best default for new systems.
gotchas.correct: OWASP lists bcrypt for legacy systems because of its 72-byte limit. New systems should use Argon2id.

gotchas.trap: Pre-hashing with SHA-512 fixes the bcrypt length limit.
gotchas.correct: OWASP warns against plain pre-hashing. Use HMAC-SHA-384 with a pepper, or move to Argon2id.

lessons.lab: Write a Node script that hashes a password with Argon2id at m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1, stores the encoded string with its parameters, and on login rehashes any hash whose stored parameters are below the current policy.

lessons.title: Passkeys, MFA and account recovery
lessons.summary: Choosing second factors that resist phishing, where passkeys fit in NIST assurance levels, and keeping account recovery from becoming the easiest way in.

sections.heading: Passkeys and WebAuthn
sections.body:
A passkey is a WebAuthn credential: a key pair whose private key stays in an authenticator (a platform authenticator, a security key, or a synced credential manager). The relying party stores only the public key. To log in, the authenticator signs a fresh server challenge, and the browser binds the credential to the relying party ID. A look-alike phishing domain cannot get a usable signature, which is why passkeys are phishing-resistant and passwords and one-time codes are not.

WebAuthn Level 3 became a W3C Recommendation in August 2026.

NIST 800-63B-4 allows **syncable authenticators** (synced passkeys) at AAL1 and AAL2 but says they **SHALL NOT** be used at AAL3. AAL3 needs a device-bound, non-exportable key, such as a hardware security key.

sections.heading: Ranking MFA options
sections.body:
From strongest to weakest for a typical app:

1. **Passkeys or security keys** (WebAuthn): phishing-resistant.
2. **Authenticator app TOTP** and push with number matching: resist SIM swap, but a real-time phishing proxy can still relay them.
3. **SMS or voice codes**: NIST calls these "restricted". You may use them only if you also offer an alternative.
4. **Email codes**: under 800-63B-4, email **SHALL NOT** be used as an out-of-band authenticator.

Out-of-band secrets must have at least 6 digits, be valid for no more than 10 minutes, and work only once.

sections.heading: Account recovery is an authentication path
sections.body:
Attackers go for the weakest route into an account, and that is often recovery. If a user has a passkey but can "recover" with a security question or an emailed link that also skips MFA, then the passkey adds little.

Recovery practices, following the OWASP Forgot Password and Multifactor Authentication cheat sheets:

- Return the same response whether or not the account exists, so the reset form cannot be used to find accounts.
- Make reset tokens random, long, single-use and short-lived. Store them hashed like any other secret.
- Encourage users to register more than one authenticator (a second passkey, or one-time recovery codes) so recovery rarely needs a weak channel.
- Notify the user on every recovery or factor change. For high-value accounts, add a delay or manual review before a factor change takes effect.
- Invalidate existing sessions after a password reset or factor change.

Security questions are not allowed as an authenticator under 800-63B-4.

keyPoints: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser scopes each credential to the relying party ID and the authenticator signs a fresh challenge.
Synced passkeys are fine at AAL1 and AAL2 but not at AAL3.
SMS is restricted, so you must offer an alternative. Email must not be used as an out-of-band authenticator.
Recovery has to be about as strong as login. Offer backup authenticators, single-use reset tokens, notifications, and session invalidation.

gotchas.trap: TOTP is phishing-resistant because the code changes every 30 seconds.
gotchas.correct: A real-time proxy can relay a TOTP code. Only origin-bound methods such as WebAuthn are phishing-resistant.

gotchas.trap: Emailed codes are a fine second factor for AAL2.
gotchas.correct: 800-63B-4 says email SHALL NOT be used for out-of-band authentication.

gotchas.trap: Once passkeys are deployed, recovery can stay as it was.
gotchas.correct: A weak recovery path becomes the easiest way to take over the account.

lessons.lab: Sketch the recovery flow for an app that offers passkeys. List each path into an account (login, reset, support desk, factor change) and the strongest proof each one asks for. Fix any path that is weaker than passkey login.

lessons.title: Session cookies, rotation, expiry and logout
lessons.summary: Building a session cookie that scripts cannot read, that cannot be planted by a subdomain, and that is rotated, timed out and destroyed correctly.

sections.heading: The session ID itself
sections.body: A session ID must come from a CSPRNG and carry at least **64 bits of entropy**, for example at least 16 hex characters of random data. It must not contain meaning (no user ID or timestamp). **Regenerate** the ID after login and after any privilege change, such as entering an admin mode. This defeats session fixation, where an attacker plants a known ID before the victim logs in.

sections.heading: Cookie attributes
sections.body:
A good session cookie looks like this:

```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=8f1c...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

- **Secure**: sent only over HTTPS.
- **HttpOnly**: JavaScript cannot read it, which limits the damage of XSS. The cookie is still sent automatically with fetch and XHR requests, so HttpOnly does nothing against CSRF.
- **SameSite**: Strict is preferred, Lax is acceptable. Lax still sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, but not on cross-site POSTs, fetch calls, subresources or iframes. `SameSite=None` requires `Secure`. Some browsers treat a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax, but not all do, so set it explicitly.
- **Prefixes**: `__Secure-` requires Secure. `__Host-` requires Secure, **no Domain** attribute and `Path=/`, which locks the cookie to one host so a sibling subdomain cannot overwrite it. The newer `__Http-` and `__Host-Http-` prefixes also require HttpOnly, which proves the cookie came from a Set-Cookie header and not from script.
- **Domain**: if you set it, every subdomain receives the cookie. Leave it off for session cookies.
- **Max-Age** wins over Expires when both are present.

sections.heading: Expiry and logout
sections.body:
Enforce timeouts **on the server**, not only in the cookie. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet suggests an idle timeout of 2–5 minutes for high-value applications and 15–30 minutes for low-risk ones, plus an absolute timeout (for example 4–8 hours for an office app) after which the user must log in again.

Logout must **invalidate the session on the server**. Clearing the cookie in the browser is not enough, because a copy of the ID that was stolen earlier would still work. Do the same server-side invalidation after a password reset.

Do not keep session IDs, JWTs or refresh tokens in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`. Any script running on the page can read them.

keyPoints: Use at least 64 bits of CSPRNG entropy, and regenerate the ID on login and on privilege change.
Use __Host- (or __Host-Http-) with Secure, HttpOnly, Path=/, no Domain, and SameSite=Strict or Lax.
HttpOnly blocks script reads, but the browser still sends the cookie, so add CSRF defences.
Enforce idle and absolute timeouts on the server, and invalidate the session on the server at logout.

gotchas.trap: HttpOnly prevents CSRF.
gotchas.correct: HttpOnly only stops JavaScript from reading the cookie. Browsers still attach it to requests.

gotchas.trap: Adding Domain=example.com to a __Host- cookie is harmless.
gotchas.correct: Browsers reject a __Host- cookie that has a Domain attribute.

gotchas.trap: Deleting the cookie on logout ends the session.
gotchas.correct: The server must invalidate the session ID, or any stolen copy keeps working.

lessons.lab: In an Express app, issue a __Host-sid cookie with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Path=/. Regenerate the session on login, enforce a 15-minute idle and an 8-hour absolute timeout in the session store, and confirm with curl that a replayed cookie fails after logout.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect for real apps
lessons.summary: Authorization code with PKCE, exact redirect URIs, state, nonce and iss, and where tokens should live in SPAs and mobile apps, following RFC 9700 and RFC 10017.

sections.heading: The flow to use
sections.body:
RFC 9700 (the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, January 2025) sets the baseline:

- Use the **authorization code grant with PKCE**. Public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) **MUST** use PKCE, and confidential clients are recommended to. **S256** is the only acceptable challenge method. `plain` is not acceptable, and authorization servers must stop downgrade attacks.
- The **implicit grant SHOULD NOT** be used.
- The **resource owner password credentials (ROPC) grant MUST NOT** be used.
- Access tokens **MUST NOT** be sent in a query string.

The OAuth 2.1 draft (still an Internet-Draft, not an RFC) builds these rules in: it requires PKCE and does not define the implicit or ROPC grants at all.

sections.heading: Redirect URIs
sections.body: The authorization server must compare redirect URIs using **exact string matching**. The one exception is the port on a localhost loopback redirect for native apps. Wildcards, prefix matching and "any subdomain" rules let an attacker send the authorization code to a page they control. Do not run open redirectors on your client domains either, because they can turn an exact-match URI into a leak.

sections.heading: state, nonce and iss
sections.body:
- **state**: an unguessable value tied to the user's browser session and checked on the callback. It prevents CSRF against the redirect endpoint. RFC 9700 says PKCE or the OIDC nonce is enough for CSRF protection only if you are sure the authorization server supports PKCE. Otherwise use state.
- **nonce** (OpenID Connect): sent in the authentication request and returned inside the ID token. The client checks that they match, which stops a captured ID token from being replayed.
- **iss** (RFC 9207): when a client talks to more than one authorization server, it checks the `iss` parameter in the authorization response and aborts if it does not match. This defeats mix-up attacks.

sections.heading: Where tokens live
sections.body:
**Browser apps.** RFC 10017 (August 2026) ranks three patterns:

1. **Backend for frontend (BFF)**: the server runs the OAuth flow and keeps the tokens, and the browser holds only a session cookie. This is "strongly recommended" for business, sensitive or personal data.
2. **Token-mediating backend**: the backend gets the tokens and hands access tokens to the browser.
3. **Browser-only public client**: the weakest option.

The BFF cookie MUST be Secure and HttpOnly. It SHOULD be SameSite=Strict, Path=/, have no Domain, and use the `__Host-Http-` prefix. If the browser does hold refresh tokens, the authorization server must rotate or sender-constrain them and cap their lifetime. DPoP limits a stolen token to online use from the victim's browser, but it cannot stop an attacker who runs a new flow inside a compromised page.

**Native apps.** Following RFC 8252, run the flow in the **system browser** (or an in-app browser tab), not an embedded web view the app can read, and use PKCE. Beyond RFC 8252, common practice is to keep tokens in the platform's secure storage (Keychain or Keystore).

RFC 9700 also says refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or rotated, and access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted and sender-constrained (mTLS or DPoP).

keyPoints: Use the authorization code grant with PKCE (S256). Never use implicit or ROPC.
Match redirect URIs exactly. Only the loopback port may vary.
state stops callback CSRF, nonce stops ID token replay, and iss stops mix-up attacks.
Use a BFF for browser apps that handle sensitive data. Native apps use the system browser and secure storage.
Public-client refresh tokens must be rotated or sender-constrained.

gotchas.trap: Implicit flow is fine for SPAs because there is no client secret.
gotchas.correct: RFC 9700 says implicit SHOULD NOT be used. SPAs use the code grant with PKCE, ideally behind a BFF.

gotchas.trap: OAuth 2.1 is an RFC.
gotchas.correct: As of November 2026 it is still an IETF draft. Cite RFC 9700 for normative guidance.

gotchas.trap: Wildcard redirect URIs are fine if they stay on your own domain.
gotchas.correct: Matching must be exact. A wildcard can reach an open redirect or a compromised subdomain.

lessons.lab: Register a test client with one exact redirect URI. Implement the code flow with PKCE S256, state and nonce checks in a small BFF that stores tokens server-side and issues a __Host-Http- session cookie. Then try a callback with a missing state and confirm it is rejected.

lessons.title: JWTs: validation, algorithm confusion and revocation
lessons.summary: When a JWT is the right tool, how to validate one so the token cannot choose its own rules, and how to cope with the fact that you cannot easily take one back.

sections.heading: When to use a JWT
sections.body: A JWT is a signed, self-contained set of claims. It is useful when one party issues tokens and many independent services verify them without a shared session store, for example access tokens for APIs or OIDC ID tokens. For a single web app with a server-side session store, an opaque random session ID in a cookie is simpler and easier to revoke. Using JWTs as browser session tokens kept in localStorage adds risk and brings no benefit.

sections.heading: Validate like you mean it
sections.body:
RFC 8725 (the JWT Best Current Practices) and common libraries come down to these rules:

- **Pin the algorithms** you accept. Never take `alg` from the token header at face value, and never accept `alg: none`.
- **Algorithm confusion**: if a verifier picks the algorithm from the header, an attacker can switch RS256 to HS256 and sign with the server's **public** key as the HMAC secret. If the verifier then feeds that public key into HMAC, the forged token passes.
- **Do not let the token pick its own key.** Treat `kid` as a lookup into your own key set only, and ignore attacker-supplied `jku` or `x5u` URLs. Fetching them can also open an SSRF hole.
- **Validate the claims**: `iss` is your expected issuer, `aud` includes this service, and `exp` (and `nbf`) are checked with a small clock skew allowance.
- Use explicit typing (the `typ` header) so one kind of JWT cannot be passed off as another.

In the jose library:

```ts
await jwtVerify(token, key, { issuer, audience, algorithms: ['HS256'] });
```

A wrong audience throws `ERR_JWT_CLAIM_VALIDATION_FAILED`.

An update to RFC 8725 (8725bis) is in progress but is not an RFC yet.

sections.heading: Revocation strategies
sections.body:
A verifier that checks only the signature will accept a JWT until it expires, even after the user logs out or the token is stolen. Common strategies:

- Keep **access tokens short-lived** (minutes) and pair them with **refresh tokens** that are checked against server state, rotated on every use, and revocable.
- Keep a **denylist** of revoked `jti` values (or a per-user "tokens issued before" timestamp) for emergencies, held only until the token's natural expiry.
- Use **token introspection** at the authorization server for high-risk APIs.
- **Rotate signing keys** if a key may have leaked, and publish the key set so verifiers pick up the change.

keyPoints: Use JWTs for cross-service verification. Use opaque cookies for a single app with a session store.
Pin algorithms, reject none, and look kid up only in your own key set.
Always validate iss, aud and exp, not just the signature.
Revoke with short access-token lifetimes, rotated refresh tokens, and a jti denylist.

gotchas.trap: A valid signature means the token is good.
gotchas.correct: A token can be correctly signed and still be for another audience, from another issuer, or expired.

gotchas.trap: Logging out deletes the JWT, so it is revoked.
gotchas.correct: A copy keeps working until exp unless the server checks a denylist or uses short lifetimes.

gotchas.trap: Supporting every algorithm the library knows is more compatible.
gotchas.correct: Accepting any algorithm makes algorithm confusion possible. Pin exactly what you issue.

lessons.lab: With jose, issue an RS256 token, then write a verifier that pins algorithms to RS256 and checks issuer and audience. Show that an HS256 token signed with the public key, a token with the wrong aud, and an expired token are all rejected.

lessons.title: Broken access control: IDOR, BOLA and tenant isolation
lessons.summary: Why broken access control tops the OWASP Top 10:2025, how object-level and function-level checks fail, and how to keep tenants apart in a multi-tenant SaaS.

sections.heading: Why access control is still number one
sections.body:
Broken Access Control is **A01:2025** in the OWASP Top 10:2025, as it was in 2021. The 2025 edition also folds Server-Side Request Forgery into A01. In the 2025 CWE Top 25, **CWE-862 Missing Authorization** is #4, **CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization** is #17 and **CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key** (the classic IDOR) is #24.

Authentication answers "who are you?". Authorization answers "may *this* user do *this* action on *this* object, right now?". Most access-control bugs are not exotic: a handler loads a record by id and never asks the second question.

sections.heading: Object-level checks: IDOR and BOLA
Function-level checks
sections.body:
**Broken Function Level Authorization** (API5:2023) is the same mistake one level up: a regular user can call an admin or privileged *operation*, for example `PATCH /api/users/:id/role`, because the only "control" is that the UI hides the button. Anyone can send the request directly.

Every privileged route needs a server-side check of the caller's role or permission, denied by default. Keep admin functions on clearly separated routes so the check is easy to apply and audit.

sections.heading: Do not authorize only at the edge
sections.body: CVE-2025-29927 in Next.js let crafted requests skip middleware entirely on self-hosted deployments. Apps that enforced authorization **only** in middleware were exposed until patched. The lesson is general: middleware, gateways and route guards are a useful first filter, but the handler or data-access layer must re-check authorization for the specific object it touches.

sections.heading: Tenant isolation in multi-tenant SaaS
sections.body:
In a shared-schema SaaS every row carries a `tenant_id`. Isolation rules:

- Derive the tenant from the **authenticated session or token**, never from a request header, query parameter or body field the client controls.
- Scope every query by tenant, ideally through one repository layer or a database control such as PostgreSQL row-level security, so a forgotten `WHERE` clause cannot leak data.
- Return **404** rather than 403 for another tenant's object so ids cannot be probed.
- Cover caches, search indexes, file storage keys, background jobs and exports, not just the main database.
- Test with two tenants: an automated test that signs in as tenant A and requests tenant B's ids should fail closed.

keyPoints: A01:2025 Broken Access Control is the top web risk and now includes SSRF.
IDOR/BOLA: check that the caller may access the specific object on every request.
Unguessable ids are defence in depth, not an authorization control.
Function-level checks belong on the server, deny by default; hiding a button is not a control.
Re-check authorization in the handler or data layer, not only in middleware.
Take tenant_id from the authenticated session and scope every data path by it.

gotchas.trap: Switching integer ids to UUIDs fixes IDOR.
gotchas.correct: UUIDs only slow guessing; the server must still verify access to each object.

gotchas.trap: The admin page is hidden from normal users, so the admin API is safe.
gotchas.correct: Attackers call the API directly; enforce the role check server-side.

gotchas.trap: Reading the tenant from an X-Tenant-Id header is fine because the user is authenticated.
gotchas.correct: Authenticated does not mean authorized for that tenant; derive tenant from the session.

lessons.lab: Build a tiny Express or Next.js route `GET /api/invoices/:id` backed by an in-memory store with two tenants. Write a test that signs in as tenant A and fetches a tenant B invoice id; watch it succeed. Fix the route so the lookup includes the session tenant and returns 404, and keep the test as a regression guard.

lessons.title: Authorization models and PostgreSQL row-level security
lessons.summary: RBAC, ABAC and relationship-based access control, why to enforce decisions in one place, and how to use PostgreSQL RLS as a tenant-isolation backstop without falling into its bypass traps.

sections.heading: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
sections.body:
- **RBAC** (role-based): permissions attach to roles such as `admin`, `editor`, `viewer`. Simple and auditable, but it struggles with per-object rules and tends toward "role explosion".
- **ABAC** (attribute-based): a policy evaluates attributes of the subject, object, action and context, for example "owner of the document, same tenant, during business hours".
- **ReBAC** (relationship-based): access follows a graph of relationships such as "user is member of group, group is editor of folder, folder contains doc". Google's Zanzibar paper describes this model at scale, and it fits sharing and inheritance well.

The OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet recommends preferring attribute- and relationship-based models over plain RBAC for anything beyond coarse roles, together with **deny by default**, least privilege and **validating permissions on every request**.

sections.heading: Enforce in one place
sections.body: Scattered `if (user.role === 'admin')` checks drift apart. Put the decision behind one function or policy service (a policy decision point), for example `can(user, 'invoice:update', invoice)`, and call it from every path that reaches the data: HTTP handlers, GraphQL resolvers, background jobs and exports. One place makes rules testable, reviewable and consistent, and the default when no rule matches is deny.

sections.heading: Row-level security basics
sections.body:
PostgreSQL row-level security adds a database-enforced filter on top of table privileges.

```sql
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  AS RESTRICTIVE
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
```

- With RLS enabled and **no policy**, access is **default-deny**.
- `USING` filters rows that are read or targeted by UPDATE/DELETE. `WITH CHECK` validates rows being written; if omitted it defaults to the `USING` expression.
- Permissive policies (the default) are **OR-ed** together; `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies are **AND-ed** with them. A tenant rule should be restrictive so a later permissive policy cannot widen it. Note that restrictive policies alone grant nothing: at least one permissive policy must also allow the row.
- With the `missing_ok` argument, `current_setting(..., true)` returns NULL when the setting is absent, so the comparison matches nothing and the query fails closed.

sections.heading: The bypass traps
sections.body:
- **Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS and (normally) the table owner bypass RLS.** If the app connects as the owner, policies do nothing. `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` makes the owner subject to them; superusers still bypass. The robust fix is an app role that owns nothing and lacks BYPASSRLS.
- **Connection pools:** a plain `SET app.tenant_id` lasts for the session, so the next request on that pooled connection inherits it. Use `SET LOCAL` (or `set_config(name, value, true)`) inside the request's transaction so it resets at commit or rollback.
- **Views** run with the view owner's privileges by default, so the owner's RLS treatment applies. Create them `WITH (security_invoker = true)` to check the calling user.
- Referential-integrity checks bypass RLS, which can reveal that a row exists.

RLS is a backstop for application checks, not a replacement for them.

keyPoints: RBAC for coarse roles; ABAC and ReBAC for per-object, sharing and inheritance rules.
Route every decision through one deny-by-default policy function.
RLS with no policy denies everything; USING filters, WITH CHECK validates writes.
Permissive policies OR together; make tenant isolation AS RESTRICTIVE.
Owners, superusers and BYPASSRLS roles skip RLS; connect as a non-owner app role.
With pooled connections set the tenant with SET LOCAL inside a transaction.

gotchas.trap: RLS is enabled, so the app is isolated even though it connects as the table owner.
gotchas.correct: The owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; use a non-owner role.

gotchas.trap: Adding another permissive policy can only narrow access.
gotchas.correct: Permissive policies are OR-ed, so each one widens access.

gotchas.trap: SET app.tenant_id at the start of each request is safe with a pool.
gotchas.correct: Session settings persist on the pooled connection; use SET LOCAL in a transaction.

lessons.lab: In the course SQL sandbox create an `invoices` table with two tenants, enable RLS and add a restrictive tenant policy plus a permissive `USING (true)` policy. The sandbox runs as superuser `postgres`, so first observe that all rows come back. Then `CREATE ROLE app_user NOLOGIN`, grant it SELECT, `SET ROLE app_user`, begin a transaction, `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id` to one tenant and confirm only that tenant's rows are returned.

lessons.title: Data protection: encryption and key management
lessons.summary: What encryption in transit and at rest each protect against, envelope encryption with a KMS, and when to add field-level encryption for secrets and PII.

sections.heading: Encryption in transit
sections.body: Use TLS for every hop that crosses a network you do not fully control, including service-to-database and service-to-service traffic, not just the browser edge. For browsers, **HSTS** tells the client to use HTTPS only; it is ignored when received over plain HTTP and has a first-visit weakness that preload lists address. Certificate validation must stay on in clients; disabling it "temporarily" removes the protection TLS provides.

sections.heading: Encryption at rest: what each layer stops
sections.body:
- **Disk, volume or managed-database storage encryption** protects against lost or stolen media and snapshots copied outside the account. It is transparent: anyone who can query the database, including an attacker using SQL injection or a stolen app credential, sees plaintext.
- **Application-level (field-level) encryption** encrypts specific values before they reach the database. A database dump, a read replica or an over-broad analytics user then sees only ciphertext; only code holding the key can decrypt.

Choose by threat: storage encryption is a cheap baseline, field-level encryption is for high-value fields such as national ids, bank details or third-party API secrets the app must reuse.

sections.heading: Envelope encryption and a KMS
sections.body:
In **envelope encryption**, a data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data and a key encryption key (KEK), held in a key management service or HSM, encrypts the DEK. You store the **encrypted DEK next to the ciphertext**; the KEK never leaves the KMS. To decrypt, the app asks the KMS to unwrap the DEK, which is logged and governed by key policy.

Benefits: large data is encrypted locally and fast, access to the KEK is centrally controlled and audited, and rotating the KEK does not require re-encrypting all data, only re-wrapping DEKs.

sections.heading: Doing field-level encryption well
sections.body:
- Use a vetted library and an **authenticated** mode such as AES-GCM, never a home-made scheme or ECB.
- Keep keys out of the database and out of source code; store them in a KMS or secrets manager, separate from the data they protect.
- Bind ciphertext to its context (for example record id as associated data) so values cannot be swapped between rows.
- Plan rotation: record which key version encrypted each value.
- **Passwords are hashed, not encrypted** (argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt). Encryption is reversible; use it only when the application must recover the original, as with a customer's third-party API secret. Tokens the app only needs to verify, such as API keys it issued, can be stored as hashes.

keyPoints: TLS on every network hop, with certificate validation on; HSTS for browsers.
Storage encryption stops lost-media threats, not queries through the app or SQL injection.
Field-level encryption keeps high-value fields as ciphertext in dumps and replicas.
Envelope encryption: DEK encrypts data, KMS-held KEK wraps the DEK; store the wrapped DEK with the data.
Use authenticated encryption and keep keys separate from data.
Hash what you only verify (passwords, issued API keys); encrypt what you must recover.

gotchas.trap: Our managed database is encrypted at rest, so a SQL injection cannot expose PII.
gotchas.correct: Storage encryption is transparent to queries; injection returns plaintext.

gotchas.trap: Encrypt user passwords with a KMS key so support can recover them.
gotchas.correct: Passwords must be hashed with a slow password hash; never reversible.

lessons.lab: Write a small Node script that generates a random 256-bit DEK, encrypts a JSON record with AES-256-GCM using the record id as associated data, then "wraps" the DEK with a second key standing in for a KMS KEK. Store wrapped DEK, IV, tag and ciphertext together, decrypt, and show that changing the associated data makes decryption fail.

lessons.title: Secrets management and responding to a leak
lessons.summary: Keep secrets out of code and images, prefer short-lived credentials, rotate on a schedule, and know the first moves when a secret leaks.

sections.heading: Never in code or images
sections.body:
Secrets in source code end up in every clone, fork, CI log and backup. Keep them in a secrets manager or the platform's secret store and inject them at runtime.

Container images are a second trap. Docker's documentation warns that **build arguments and environment variables are not appropriate for secrets** because they persist in the final image and its metadata. Use build secret mounts instead:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) npm ci
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN .
```

sections.heading: Short-lived credentials beat stored keys
sections.body: A long-lived access key in a CI variable is valid until someone remembers to revoke it. Prefer **temporary credentials**: AWS IAM roles issue credentials that expire automatically, and CI systems that support OpenID Connect can exchange a signed identity token for a role session, so no cloud key is stored at all. Scope each role to the minimum actions and resources, and restrict which repository and branch may assume it.

sections.heading: Rotation
sections.body: Rotate secrets on a schedule and on every suspected exposure or staff change. Rotation is only practical if it is automated and the app can hold **two valid versions at once** (current and previous) during cut-over. Managed secret stores can run rotation functions for databases and other services. A secret that cannot be rotated without downtime is a finding in itself.

sections.heading: When a secret leaks
sections.body:
GitHub's guidance after secret scanning finds a credential is to **rotate the affected credential immediately**; rewriting git history is "often unnecessary if you've already revoked the credential". Order of work:

1. **Revoke or rotate** the secret at the provider. Assume it is already copied.
2. Check provider logs for use of the credential since exposure and contain any misuse.
3. Remove it from the code going forward and fix the path that let it in.
4. Only then consider history rewriting, mainly for hygiene.

Detection helps: GitHub secret scanning is free on public repositories; for private organization repositories it is part of **GitHub Secret Protection**. Validity checks show whether a found secret is still live, and partner providers may be notified and may revoke. **Push protection** blocks pushes that contain recognized secrets; a bypass marked "used in tests" or "false positive" closes the alert, while "I'll fix it later" leaves an open alert.

The 2025 tj-actions/changed-files compromise, where release tags were repointed to a malicious commit that dumped CI secrets, is a reminder: CISA advised rotating the exposed secrets, and GitHub recommends pinning third-party actions to a full-length commit SHA, which limits this class of attack.

keyPoints: No secrets in source, build args or image environment; use runtime injection and build secret mounts.
Prefer temporary credentials from roles and OIDC federation over stored keys.
Automate rotation and support two valid versions during cut-over.
On a leak: revoke or rotate first, then investigate use, then clean up.
Push protection blocks known secrets; "I'll fix it later" bypasses leave an open alert.

gotchas.trap: Force-pushing to remove the leaked key from history fixes the leak.
gotchas.correct: Copies may already exist; revoke or rotate the credential first.

gotchas.trap: Passing a token as a Docker build ARG is fine if the final stage does not use it.
gotchas.correct: Build args persist in image metadata; use --mount=type=secret.

lessons.lab: Take a Dockerfile that uses `ARG NPM_TOKEN`, build it with a dummy token and run `docker history --no-trunc` to find the value. Rewrite it with a `--mount=type=secret` step, rebuild and confirm the value no longer appears in history or `docker inspect`.

lessons.title: Privacy engineering basics
lessons.summary: Data minimisation, retention and deletion, audit trails that do not become a second leak, and the GDPR 72-hour breach clock.

sections.heading: Minimisation by design
sections.body:
GDPR Article 5 lists **data minimisation** ("adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary") and **storage limitation** (kept identifiable "no longer than is necessary") among its core principles. For engineers this means:

- Do not collect a field without a stated purpose. Ask "what breaks if we do not store this?"
- Strip or truncate data at the edge: log a user id instead of an email, the last four digits instead of a full card or account number.
- Keep analytics and logs free of request bodies by default; add fields deliberately.
- Pseudonymise where a stable key is needed but identity is not.

Data you never stored cannot leak, cannot be subpoenaed and does not need deleting.

sections.heading: Retention and deletion
sections.body:
Give every data set an owner and a retention period, and enforce it in code: TTL indexes, partition drops, lifecycle rules on object storage and scheduled purge jobs. Deletion must reach **every copy**: replicas, search indexes, caches, data warehouse tables, exports and third-party processors. Backups usually expire on their own schedule, so document how long deleted data survives there.

Article 17 gives individuals a right to erasure in defined circumstances. A deletion pipeline keyed by user id, with a record of what was deleted and when, makes such requests routine rather than a manual hunt.

sections.heading: Audit trails
sections.body: An audit trail records security-relevant actions, such as admin access to customer records, permission changes, exports and deletions: **who** (actor id), **what** (action and target id), **when**, **from where** and the **outcome**. It should be append-only for the application (written to a store the app cannot update or delete) and should avoid copying the sensitive values themselves. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet also lists data that should not be logged directly, such as session ids, access tokens, passwords and sensitive personal data, which should be removed, masked or hashed instead.

sections.heading: The breach clock
sections.body: Under GDPR Article 33 a controller notifies the supervisory authority "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than **72 hours after having become aware**" of a personal data breach, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals. Late notifications must explain the delay, information may be provided in phases, and a processor must tell the controller without undue delay. Engineering's part is to have the logs and data inventory that let the team answer "what data, whose, how many" within that window. Other regimes, such as US state laws and SEC rules for public companies, have different triggers and deadlines.

keyPoints: Collect only what a stated purpose needs; minimise at the edge.
Every data set has an owner and an enforced retention period.
Deletion must reach replicas, indexes, caches, warehouses and processors.
Audit trails: who, what, when, where, outcome; append-only; no secrets or raw PII.
GDPR Art. 33: notify within 72 hours of becoming aware, where feasible; phased information is allowed.

gotchas.trap: Logs are encrypted, so keeping full request bodies forever is fine.
gotchas.correct: Encryption does not satisfy minimisation or storage limitation; drop and expire data.

gotchas.trap: The 72 hours start when the investigation is complete.
gotchas.correct: They start when the controller becomes aware of the breach.

For each field write its purpose and retention period, mark fields with no purpose for removal, and add a scheduled purge (for example a daily `DELETE ... WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days'`) plus a log redaction rule for emails.

lessons.title: Injection: SQL, NoSQL and OS commands
lessons.summary: Why injection happens, how to build queries and commands so data can never become code, and why an ORM does not make you safe by itself.

sections.heading: The root cause: mixing code and data
sections.body:
Injection is A05:2025 in the OWASP Top 10, and in the 2025 CWE Top 25 SQL injection (CWE-89) ranks #2 and OS command injection (CWE-78) ranks #9. Every variant has the same shape: untrusted input is concatenated into a string that another interpreter (a SQL engine, a shell, a query language) parses as code.

The fix is also the same shape: send code and data to the interpreter **separately**, so the input can never change the structure of the statement. Input validation and escaping are useful layers, but they are not the primary defense.

sections.heading: Parameterized queries and their limits
ORMs are not automatic protection
sections.body: ORMs and query builders parameterize the queries they generate, which is why they help. But every ORM also has escape hatches: raw query methods, raw fragments in `where` or `orderBy`, and string-built filters. Concatenating input into any of these is exactly as vulnerable as hand-written SQL. Review raw-query call sites in code review and use the ORM's own binding syntax inside them.

sections.heading: NoSQL injection
OS command injection and argument injection

keyPoints: Separate code from data: bound parameters for SQL, argument arrays without a shell for commands.
Identifiers and keywords (columns, tables, ASC/DESC) cannot be bound; map them through an allowlist.
ORM raw-query APIs and raw fragments are as injectable as hand-written SQL.
NoSQL injection is often operator injection; validate input type and shape with a schema.
An argument array blocks shell metacharacters but not option injection; validate and use -- where supported.

gotchas.trap: We use an ORM, so we cannot have SQL injection.
gotchas.correct: ORMs parameterize generated queries, but raw query methods and raw fragments built by concatenation are still injectable.

gotchas.trap: Escaping single quotes is a good enough SQL injection fix.
gotchas.correct: Use bound parameters; hand-rolled escaping is fragile and database-specific. OWASP treats escaping as a last resort.

gotchas.trap: Binding the column name as a parameter makes dynamic ORDER BY safe.
gotchas.correct: Parameters bind values, not identifiers; map the input to an allowlisted column name in code.

gotchas.trap: spawn with an argument array makes any input safe.
gotchas.correct: It prevents shell injection but not argument injection; a value like --output=/etc/x can still be read as an option.

lessons.lab: Write a small Node.js endpoint that searches a PostgreSQL table by name and sorts by a user-chosen column. Implement it once with string concatenation and show that a crafted value changes the query, then rewrite it with a bound parameter for the search term and an allowlist map for the sort column and direction. Finally, add a route that runs a command with execFile and an argument array, and try a value that starts with a dash.

lessons.title: Cross-site scripting and output encoding
lessons.summary: XSS is the #1 weakness in the 2025 CWE Top 25. Learn the output contexts, the right encoding for each, how to sanitize user HTML, and the framework escape hatches that switch protection off.

sections.heading: Why XSS still tops the list
sections.body: Cross-site scripting (CWE-79) is #1 in the 2025 CWE Top 25. A script injected into your origin runs with the user's session: it can read the page, call your APIs as the user and change what they see. Reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS differ in where the payload comes from, but the defense is the same: untrusted data must never be interpreted as markup or code.

sections.heading: Encode for the output context
sections.body:
The OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet is built around **contexts**. The same value needs different encoding depending on where it lands:

- **HTML body**: HTML entity encoding.
- **Quoted HTML attribute**: attribute encoding, and always quote the attribute.
- **JavaScript**: avoid placing untrusted data in scripts at all. Put it in a data attribute or a JSON block and read it with `JSON.parse`.
- **CSS**: never interpolate. Use `style.setProperty` with an allowlisted value.
- **URL**: percent-encode the parameter, then attribute-encode the whole attribute. Validate the scheme of full URLs (allow `https:`, reject `javascript:`).

HTML-encoding a value does not make it safe inside a script block or a URL.

sections.heading: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
sections.body:
Modern frameworks escape text by default, which removes most XSS. The bugs come from the escape hatches: React `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, Angular `bypassSecurityTrustAs*` and Lit `unsafeHTML`. Treat each use as a security review point.

URLs are another gap. According to the OWASP cheat sheet, React 19 blocks `javascript:` URLs in `src` and `href`, but that "does not replace application-specific URL validation". Parse user URLs with `new URL()` and allow only the schemes you expect.

sections.heading: Sanitizing user HTML and the DOM
sections.body:
When users must supply rich HTML, sanitize it with a well-maintained library such as **DOMPurify** right before insertion, and do not modify the HTML after sanitizing it (that can reintroduce dangerous markup). Sanitize the final HTML, for example after Markdown has been converted, not the input to the converter.

For DOM code, prefer safe sinks: `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`, `setAttribute` for non-event attributes. Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'` in CSP) can make dangerous sinks reject plain strings, which turns DOM XSS review into a small, auditable set of policies.

keyPoints: Encoding depends on the output context: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, CSS and URL each differ.
Keep untrusted data out of script blocks; pass it via data attributes or JSON and parse it.
dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustAs* and unsafeHTML switch off framework escaping.
Sanitize user HTML with DOMPurify immediately before insertion and do not modify it afterwards.
Prefer textContent over innerHTML; validate URL schemes for href and src.

gotchas.trap: Our template engine HTML-escapes everything, so values inside inline scripts are safe.
gotchas.correct: HTML encoding is the wrong context for JavaScript; move data out of scripts into a data attribute or JSON block.

gotchas.trap: React escapes output, so href={user.url} is safe.
gotchas.correct: React escapes text, but a URL needs scheme validation; React 19 blocking javascript: URLs does not replace application URL validation.

gotchas.trap: Sanitize the Markdown input before converting it to HTML.
gotchas.correct: Sanitize the final HTML output immediately before inserting it into the page.

lessons.lab: Build a tiny React page that renders a user bio from Markdown. First render the converted HTML with dangerouslySetInnerHTML and show that an img tag with an onerror handler runs. Then sanitize the converted HTML with DOMPurify right before rendering, add a profile link that only accepts https URLs parsed with new URL(), and confirm a javascript: link is rejected.

lessons.title: Content Security Policy that actually stops XSS
lessons.summary: How a strict CSP with nonces or hashes works, what strict-dynamic does, how to roll out with reporting, and why unsafe-inline undermines the whole policy.

sections.heading: What CSP is for
sections.body: CSP is a defense-in-depth layer: if an XSS bug slips through, the browser refuses to run scripts the policy does not trust. It does not replace output encoding. A policy only helps if it blocks **injected inline script**, which is what most XSS payloads are.

sections.heading: Strict CSP with nonces or hashes
sections.body:
MDN describes a strict CSP as a nonce- or hash-based `script-src` plus `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-R4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
```

- A **nonce** is a random value generated fresh for every response and placed on each legitimate script tag. Because it must be unique per response, it cannot be used in static or cached HTML.
- A **hash** allows an inline script whose content hashes to the listed value. Hashes suit static pages.
- `'strict-dynamic'` passes trust from a nonced or hashed script to the scripts it loads, which removes the need for long, bypass-prone host allowlists.

sections.heading: Why unsafe-inline undermines CSP
sections.body:
`'unsafe-inline'` allows every inline script and event handler, including the ones an attacker injects, so a policy that relies on it gives almost no XSS protection. When a nonce or hash is present, browsers **ignore** `'unsafe-inline'`, so you can list it only as a fallback for very old browsers. Note that `'unsafe-eval'` still takes effect alongside nonces and hashes.

Other useful directives: `frame-ancestors` (clickjacking), `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` (DOM XSS) and `upgrade-insecure-requests`, which does not replace HSTS.

sections.heading: Rolling out with reporting
sections.body:
Deploy the policy first as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, which reports violations without blocking. This header cannot be set with a `<meta>` tag, so send it from the server.

For reports, MDN recommends `report-to` with a `Reporting-Endpoints` header; `report-uri` is deprecated, but sending both for now covers older browsers. Reports arrive as `application/reports+json` with type `csp-violation`. Fix the violations, then switch to the enforcing header.

keyPoints: Strict CSP: nonce or hash in script-src, plus object-src none and base-uri none.
Nonces must be unique per response; use hashes for static or cached HTML.
strict-dynamic extends trust to scripts loaded by trusted scripts.
unsafe-inline lets injected inline script run; it is ignored when a nonce or hash is present.
Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only (header only) and report-to with Reporting-Endpoints.

gotchas.trap: A fixed nonce baked into the HTML template is fine.
gotchas.correct: A nonce must be unpredictable and unique per response, otherwise an attacker can reuse it.

gotchas.trap: Put Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only in a meta tag to test.
gotchas.correct: Report-Only cannot be delivered via meta; send it as a response header.

gotchas.trap: report-uri is the standard way to collect CSP reports.
gotchas.correct: report-uri is deprecated; use report-to with Reporting-Endpoints, and keep report-uri only as a fallback.

lessons.lab: Serve a page from a small Node.js server that generates a fresh random nonce per request and sets a strict CSP with nonce, strict-dynamic, object-src none and base-uri none. Add an inline script with the nonce and one without, and check in the browser console which one is blocked. Then switch to the Report-Only header with a Reporting-Endpoints endpoint and log the violation reports you receive.

lessons.title: CSRF, SameSite, CORS and clickjacking
lessons.summary: How browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests, the CSRF defenses OWASP recommends today, why SameSite and CORS are not CSRF defenses on their own, and how to stop framing.

sections.heading: CSRF and the defenses that work
sections.body:
CSRF abuses the browser attaching cookies to requests another site triggers. The OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends:

- A **synchronizer token**: a per-session (or per-request) secret embedded in forms and checked on state-changing requests.
- A **signed double-submit cookie**: a token bound to the session with an HMAC. The naive double-submit pattern (a random cookie echoed in a field) is discouraged.
- **Fetch Metadata**: for apps that only support modern browsers, reject cross-site state-changing requests using `Sec-Fetch-Site`, with an Origin/Referer check as fallback.
- **Custom request headers** for APIs, which rely on the CORS preflight that cross-origin custom headers trigger.

Also defend **login CSRF** (forcing a victim into the attacker's account) with pre-session tokens, and never change state with GET.

sections.heading: SameSite is defense in depth
sections.body: The `SameSite` cookie attribute limits when cookies are sent with cross-site requests. `Strict` never sends them cross-site; `Lax` still sends them on top-level navigations with safe methods such as GET; `None` requires `Secure`. OWASP is explicit that SameSite "does not replace a proper CSRF defense". "Site" is also broader than "origin": a sibling subdomain is same-site, so a compromised or user-content subdomain is not stopped by SameSite.

sections.heading: CORS misconfigurations
sections.body:
CORS relaxes the same-origin policy so that chosen origins can **read** responses. It is not a CSRF defense: a simple cross-site form POST is still sent; CORS only stops the attacker reading the reply.

Common mistakes:
- Reflecting any `Origin` back with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, which lets every site read authenticated responses.
- Suffix or regex checks that match `evilexample.com` when you meant `example.com`.
- Allowing the `null` origin, which sandboxed documents and `data:` URLs can send; MDN says `null` should not be used.

Browsers reject the wildcard `*` for credentialed requests. Use an exact-match allowlist of origins and send `Vary: Origin` when the response depends on it.

sections.heading: Clickjacking and frame-ancestors
sections.body: Clickjacking loads your page in an invisible frame and tricks the user into clicking it. The modern control is the CSP `frame-ancestors` directive (`'none'` to forbid framing, `'self'` for same-origin only), which replaces `X-Frame-Options`; sending both covers older browsers. `frame-ancestors` must be sent as a response header, not a meta tag, and JavaScript frame-busting code is not a reliable defense.

keyPoints: Primary CSRF defenses: synchronizer token, signed double-submit, Fetch Metadata with Origin fallback.
SameSite helps but does not replace a CSRF defense; Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations.
CORS controls who can read responses, not whether requests are sent.
Never reflect arbitrary origins with credentials; use an exact-match allowlist and Vary: Origin.
Use CSP frame-ancestors as a response header to stop clickjacking.

gotchas.trap: SameSite=Lax is the default, so we do not need CSRF tokens.
gotchas.correct: OWASP treats SameSite as defense in depth; keep a real CSRF defense and never change state with GET.

gotchas.trap: Our CORS policy only allows our frontend, so CSRF is impossible.
gotchas.correct: CORS does not stop simple cross-site requests being sent; it only blocks reading the response.

gotchas.trap: A random cookie echoed in a form field is enough.
gotchas.correct: Naive double-submit is discouraged; bind the token to the session with an HMAC, or use a synchronizer token.

lessons.lab: Build an Express app with a cookie session and a POST /transfer route. From a second origin, show that an auto-submitting form succeeds. Add a check that rejects requests where Sec-Fetch-Site is cross-site (falling back to an Origin check when the header is missing) and confirm the attack fails. Then add a CORS middleware that reflects any Origin with credentials, read a private JSON response from the second origin, and fix it with an exact-match allowlist.
