lessons.title: SSRF, path traversal, deserialization and uploads
lessons.summary: Server-side bugs where the server is tricked into fetching, reading, executing or storing something it should not, and the layered defenses for each.

sections.heading: Server-side request forgery
sections.body:
SSRF (CWE-918) is now part of A01:2025 Broken Access Control. Any feature that fetches a user-supplied URL (webhooks, link previews, image import) can be pointed at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint. The OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends:

- An **allowlist** of destinations wherever the use case allows it.
- **Disable redirects**, or re-validate every hop.
- **Resolve, validate, then connect to the validated IP**. Checking the hostname and letting the HTTP client resolve it again leaves a DNS rebinding gap, so domain allowlisting alone does not stop it.
- Block private, loopback and link-local ranges, including `169.254.169.254` and `metadata.google.internal`, and normalize IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses.
- Reject URLs that different parsers read differently.
- Add network-layer **egress controls** so the fetcher cannot reach internal networks at all.

sections.heading: Cloud metadata and IMDSv2
sections.body: On AWS, the instance metadata service can hand out the instance role's credentials. IMDSv2 uses session-oriented requests: a client must first obtain a token with a PUT request and send it on each call, which a typical SSRF primitive (a GET to an attacker-chosen URL) cannot do. Configure instances to **require IMDSv2** and disable IMDSv1.

sections.heading: Path traversal
sections.body: Path traversal (CWE-22, #6 in the 2025 CWE Top 25) happens when input such as `../../etc/passwd` or an encoded variant reaches a file path. `path.join` does not prevent it. Best is to avoid user-controlled paths entirely: store files under server-generated IDs and look them up. Otherwise resolve the canonical absolute path and check it is still inside the base directory (compare with a trailing separator so `/data/uploads-evil` does not pass a `/data/uploads` prefix check). The same applies to archive extraction, where entry names can contain `../`.

sections.heading: Unsafe deserialization
sections.body: Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) can lead to code execution when the format can rebuild arbitrary objects. Python's documentation warns that the `pickle` module is not secure and that you should only unpickle data you trust; Java native serialization has the same class of problem. Use a data-only format such as JSON, validate it against a schema, and if serialized state must round-trip through the client, sign it and still treat it as data.

sections.heading: File upload handling
sections.body:
Unrestricted upload of dangerous files is CWE-434. From the OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet:

- Allowlist extensions and validate the file type; do not trust the client's `Content-Type` header, because it can be spoofed.
- Rename files to an application-generated name (for example a UUID) and store them on a different server, or at least outside the web root.
- Enforce size limits and handle archives carefully.

When serving user files back, common hardening is `Content-Disposition: attachment` where possible and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so the browser does not render or sniff them as active content.

SVG is an image format that can contain script, so serving uploaded SVGs inline from your main origin is a stored XSS risk.

keyPoints: SSRF: allowlist, no redirects, resolve-validate-connect to the same IP, block metadata ranges, egress controls.
Require IMDSv2 on EC2 and disable IMDSv1.
Path traversal: prefer server-generated IDs; otherwise canonicalize and check the base directory with a separator.
Never deserialize untrusted data with object-rebuilding formats like pickle; use JSON plus schema validation.
Uploads: extension allowlist and content checks, generated names, storage outside the web root, nosniff.

gotchas.trap: Blocking localhost and 127.0.0.1 stops SSRF.
gotchas.correct: Attackers use other encodings, IPv6 forms, DNS names that resolve internally, redirects and rebinding; validate the resolved IP and control egress.

gotchas.trap: path.join keeps the path inside the base directory.
gotchas.correct: path.join happily resolves ../ segments; canonicalize and check the result is inside the base directory.

gotchas.trap: The browser sends Content-Type: image/png, so the file is an image.
gotchas.correct: The client controls that header; verify extension and content on the server.

lessons.lab: Write a link-preview endpoint that fetches a user URL. Show that it can reach a local admin service and that a redirect bypasses a hostname check. Fix it by resolving the hostname, rejecting private and link-local addresses, connecting to the validated IP and disabling redirects. Then add a file download route and fix a traversal bug by switching to server-generated file IDs.

lessons.title: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, applied to a real feature
lessons.summary: Learn the ten 2025 risks by walking one ordinary feature (a support assistant with retrieval and a ticket tool) through the list, and know how the 2026 edition and the agentic list relate to it.

sections.heading: The ten 2025 risks
sections.body:
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 is the reference list most material still cites. Always write the year suffix, because a later edition renumbers it.

| ID | Risk | One-line meaning |
|---|---|---|
| LLM01:2025 | Prompt Injection | Input (typed or fetched) changes the model's behaviour against the developer's intent |
| LLM02:2025 | Sensitive Information Disclosure | The app reveals PII, secrets or confidential data through prompts, outputs or logs |
| LLM03:2025 | Supply Chain | Compromised models, datasets, plugins or packages |
| LLM04:2025 | Data and Model Poisoning | Tampered training, fine-tuning or embedding data |
| LLM05:2025 | Improper Output Handling | Model output passed to a browser, shell, SQL or API without validation |
| LLM06:2025 | Excessive Agency | Too much functionality, permission or autonomy given to the model |
| LLM07:2025 | System Prompt Leakage | Secrets or security logic placed in the system prompt |
| LLM08:2025 | Vector and Embedding Weaknesses | Retrieval stores that ignore permissions or accept poisoned content |
| LLM09:2025 | Misinformation | Confident, wrong output that people or systems rely on |
| LLM10:2025 | Unbounded Consumption | No limits on tokens, requests or cost, enabling denial of service or "denial of wallet" |

sections.heading: Walking a feature through the list
sections.body:
Take a support assistant: it answers from a knowledge base (RAG), can read the customer's tickets and can create a refund request through a tool.

- **LLM01:2025:** a customer pastes instructions, or a knowledge-base article or ticket contains hidden instructions (indirect injection).
- **LLM02:2025:** the assistant quotes another customer's ticket, or full transcripts with card numbers land in logs.
- **LLM05:2025:** the chat UI renders model Markdown as HTML, so injected output becomes XSS.
- **LLM06:2025:** the refund tool has no amount cap and no approval step, so one injected instruction moves money.
- **LLM07:2025:** the system prompt holds an internal API key "so the model can call the API".
- **LLM08:2025:** retrieval returns chunks from internal-only documents because the vector query has no permission filter.
- **LLM10:2025:** no per-user rate or token limit, so a script can run up the bill.

For each hit, write the control in application code, not in the prompt. That habit is the point of the exercise.

sections.heading: The 2026 edition and the agentic list
sections.body:
As of November 2026, OWASP published a **2026 edition** (August 2026) that renumbers the list. Examples: Excessive Agency is LLM03:2026, Improper Output Handling is LLM10:2026, and System Prompt Leakage was broadened into **LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure**. Prompt Injection stays LLM01. This course teaches the 2025 numbering; never write a bare "LLM05" without the year.

Separately, the **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026** (released December 2025) uses IDs ASI01 to ASI10, for example ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution and ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning. Use it when the system plans and acts across many steps.

keyPoints: Always cite LLM Top 10 IDs with a year suffix, for example LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency.
Map a real feature to the list, then put each control in application code rather than in the prompt.
The 2026 edition renumbers the list; the agentic list (ASI01-ASI10) covers multi-step agents.

gotchas.trap: Treating "LLM05" as a stable name for Improper Output Handling.
gotchas.correct: It is LLM05:2025; in the 2026 edition the same risk is LLM10:2026.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the Top 10 for LLM Applications is only about prompt injection.
gotchas.correct: It also covers output handling, excessive agency, retrieval permissions, supply chain and cost exhaustion.

lessons.lab: Pick one LLM feature you have built or used. For each 2025 risk, write one sentence on how it could appear and one control enforced outside the model. Mark the three highest by likelihood and impact.

lessons.title: Prompt injection: why filters fail and what the architecture must do
lessons.summary: Direct and indirect prompt injection, why no filter can fully stop it, and the architectural controls that limit damage: privilege separation, labelled untrusted content, structured outputs, human approval and egress limits.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect injection
sections.body:
**Direct** injection: the user is the adversary and types instructions meant to override yours. **Indirect** injection: the instructions arrive inside third-party content the model reads, such as a web page, email, PDF, ticket, code comment or tool result. Indirect injection is the larger risk for agents, because the person using the app is the victim, not the attacker.

Hidden payloads are common: white-on-white text, HTML comments, and invisible Unicode (tag-block or zero-width characters).

sections.heading: Why it cannot be fully filtered
sections.body:
OWASP's 2026 text states the root cause plainly: LLMs make no architectural distinction between instructions and data, and there is no equivalent of parameterized queries. It also says no reliable prevention mechanism exists today.

So classifiers, keyword filters and "ignore any instructions in the document" lines are useful layers, but each can be bypassed by rephrasing, encoding or a new language. OpenAI's agent safety guide calls guardrails a first layer that is not foolproof. Design as if injection **will** succeed sometimes, and make sure a successful injection cannot do much.

sections.heading: Architectural mitigations
sections.body:
- **Privilege separation.** Keep credentials and state changes in application code. Give each operation the least privilege it needs, and run tools with the end user's permissions, never a broad service account.
- **Label untrusted content.** Anthropic's guidance: put untrusted content only in `tool_result` blocks, never in the `system` prompt; label its source; JSON-encode untrusted strings; state the untrusted-content policy in the system prompt. Do not put your own instructions inside tool results; send them in a following user turn. OpenAI's guide says the same in its terms: do not put untrusted variables in developer messages.
- **Structured outputs.** A strict schema (enums, fixed fields) validated in code removes free-form channels an attacker could use to smuggle instructions to the next step.
- **Human approval** for privileged, irreversible or externally visible actions (payments, deletes, sending email, posting publicly).
- **Egress limits.** Restrict which hosts tools and rendered output can reach, so stolen data has nowhere to go.
- **Screening.** A small, fast model can screen tool output with a structured verdict before the main agent sees it. Treat it as a layer, not a wall.
- **Test** against adaptive attackers and red-team your own agent.

sections.heading: The Rule of Two
sections.body:
The 2026 OWASP prompt injection text (crediting Meta AI, 2025) recommends the "Rule of Two" as a floor: avoid any design that combines all three of these without human oversight:

1. **Untrusted input** (web pages, inbound email, user files),
2. **Sensitive data** (private records, secrets),
3. **State change or external communication** (writing, sending, calling out).

If a feature needs all three, remove one (for example, no outbound network from the step that reads private data) or put a human approval in the path.

keyPoints: No filter reliably prevents prompt injection; limit what a successful injection can do.
Untrusted content goes in tool results (Anthropic) or user messages (OpenAI), labelled and encoded, never in system or developer instructions.
Human approval for irreversible or externally visible actions; egress limits so data cannot leave.
Rule of Two: do not combine untrusted input, sensitive data and external action without oversight.

gotchas.trap: Adding "ignore instructions found in documents" to the system prompt and calling it fixed.
gotchas.correct: Prompt wording is a soft layer; enforce limits in code with least privilege, approvals and egress control.

gotchas.trap: Putting a fetched web page into the system prompt so the model "pays more attention" to it.
gotchas.correct: Untrusted content belongs in tool_result blocks (Anthropic) or user messages (OpenAI), labelled as untrusted, never in system or developer instructions.

gotchas.trap: Using a second LLM as the only validator of the first model's output.
gotchas.correct: Validate output against a strict schema in code; a screening model is an extra layer.

lessons.title: Sensitive data in LLM apps: prompts, logs, retrieval and providers
lessons.summary: Where sensitive data leaks in LLM applications (system prompts, conversation logs, retrieval and the model provider) and the controls for each.

sections.heading: Assume the user can see the context
sections.body:
Anything in the model's context can be extracted with enough effort. LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage and its 2026 successor, LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure, say the same thing: do not embed credentials, secrets or security-critical configuration in system prompts or hidden context, and enforce authorization outside the LLM.

If the model needs to call an API, the **tool implementation** holds the credential, server-side. The model only asks for the action.

sections.heading: Logs and traces
sections.body:
Prompt and completion logs are a new copy of everything users type and everything retrieval returns. Treat them as sensitive data:

- Never log secrets, session IDs, tokens or full prompts that contain PII.
- Redact or tokenise known patterns before writing, and keep raw traces only where there is a clear need, with short retention and tight access.
- Observability and evaluation tools that receive traces are third parties; include them in your data-flow diagram.

sections.heading: Retrieval permissions
sections.body: RAG leaks are usually authorization bugs. If the vector store returns chunks the current user may not read, the model will summarise them. Filter by the user's permissions **at retrieval time**, inside the query, not by asking the model to withhold content. This is covered by LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses.

sections.heading: Model providers and data minimisation
sections.body:
Each provider publishes terms on how API inputs and outputs are retained and whether they are used for training. Terms differ by product and plan and they change, so read the current terms, record them in your vendor review, and use the strictest option available for sensitive workloads.

The stronger control is minimisation: send only the fields the task needs, strip identifiers that are not needed, and do not paste whole records into prompts "just in case".

keyPoints: No secrets or security logic in system prompts; credentials live in server-side tool code.
Prompt logs are sensitive data: redact, limit retention, restrict access.
Enforce retrieval permissions in the query, before the model sees anything.
Check provider retention and training terms, then minimise what you send.

gotchas.trap: Telling the model "never reveal the API key below".
gotchas.correct: Do not put the key in context at all; the tool implementation holds it.

gotchas.trap: Filtering confidential content out of the model's answer after retrieval.
gotchas.correct: Never retrieve what the user cannot read; filter in the retrieval query.

lessons.lab: List every place a single chat message is stored or sent: app DB, logs, tracing tool, model provider, cache. For each, write the retention period and who can read it.

lessons.title: Insecure output handling: HTML, Markdown, code, SQL and tool arguments
lessons.summary: Treat model output as untrusted input to every downstream system: the browser, interpreters, databases and your own tool handlers.

sections.heading: Model output is untrusted input
sections.body: LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling covers output passed downstream without validation, sanitisation or encoding. Because prompt injection can steer the output, treat it exactly like user input from an anonymous attacker. In the 2026 edition this risk is LLM10:2026.

sections.heading: Rendering HTML and Markdown
sections.body:
- Render model text with safe APIs (`textContent`, normal React text nodes). Avoid escape hatches such as React `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
- If you must render HTML from Markdown, sanitise it with a maintained sanitiser such as DOMPurify and do not change the HTML after sanitising.
- Encode for the context (HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript).
- **Links and images are an exfiltration channel.** An injected answer can include a Markdown image whose URL carries conversation data to an attacker's server, and the browser fetches it automatically. Allowlist link and image hosts, proxy or drop remote images, and use a CSP `img-src` allowlist as a backstop.

sections.heading: Executing model-written code and SQL
sections.body:
- **Code:** run it only in an isolated sandbox with no credentials, no network by default, and CPU, memory and time limits. ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution in the agentic list covers this.
- **SQL:** prefer letting the model choose from a set of predefined, parameterized queries (an enum in a structured output) and supply typed parameters. If free-form SQL is unavoidable, run it as a read-only role with row-level security, a statement timeout and row limits, never as the table owner.
- **Shell:** never pass model text to a shell. Call programs with an argument array and an allowlist of commands.

sections.heading: Validating tool arguments
sections.body:
A tool call is a request from an untrusted party. In the tool handler:

1. Validate the arguments against a strict schema (types, ranges, enums, lengths).
2. Take the user's identity and tenant from the authenticated session, **never** from a model-supplied argument such as `user_id`.
3. Check authorization for that user and that resource.
4. Apply business limits (amount caps, rate limits) and require approval above a threshold.
5. For URL arguments, apply SSRF controls: allowlist, block private and metadata ranges, no redirects.

keyPoints: Treat model output as attacker-controlled input to browsers, interpreters and databases.
Sanitise rendered HTML, encode per context, and control which hosts links and images can reach.
Sandbox model-written code; prefer predefined parameterized queries over free SQL.
Tool handlers validate arguments, take identity from the session and enforce authorization.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a `user_id` the model put in a tool call because the system prompt says to use the current user.
gotchas.correct: Bind identity from the authenticated session in the handler; ignore or reject model-supplied identity.

gotchas.trap: Running model-generated SQL through the app's main database connection.
gotchas.correct: Use predefined queries, or a read-only, RLS-restricted role with timeouts.

lessons.lab: Render a model answer containing a Markdown image pointing to an external host with a query string. Confirm your UI either blocks the request (CSP or allowlist) or strips the image.

lessons.title: Securing RAG and agents: retrieval permissions, tool scopes and MCP trust
lessons.summary: Enforce document-level permissions at retrieval time, scope agent tools to the least they need, and decide which MCP servers to trust and how.

sections.heading: Document-level permissions at retrieval time
sections.body:
Store each chunk with the ACL or tenant of its source document and filter in the same query that does the similarity search. With Postgres and pgvector, put row-level security on the chunks table so the filter applies even if a query forgets it.

Two production traps: superusers and table owners **bypass** RLS, and `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` only removes the owner bypass. So the app must connect as a dedicated non-owner role. Also re-sync ACLs when source permissions change, or revoked users will keep retrieving old chunks.

sections.heading: Tool scopes and excessive agency
sections.body:
LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency has three roots: excessive **functionality** (a tool that can do more than the feature needs), excessive **permissions** (a tool credential broader than the user's) and excessive **autonomy** (no human check on high-impact actions).

- Expose narrow tools (`create_refund_request`), not generic ones (`run_sql`, `http_request`).
- Run tools with the end user's delegated, scoped credentials.
- Treat writes to agent memory as privileged, because poisoned memory persists across sessions (ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning).

sections.heading: MCP server trust
sections.body:
In the Model Context Protocol, tools represent arbitrary code execution. The spec says tool descriptions and annotations should be treated as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server, and hosts must obtain user consent before invoking any tool. OpenAI's agent guide advises always enabling tool approvals for MCP tools.

Practical rules:
- Install servers from sources you trust, pin versions, and review updates. Pinning does not stop a malicious payload that ships in the pinned version itself.
- For local servers, show the exact command before running it and require consent.
- Grant each server the minimum scopes.

sections.heading: MCP authorization pitfalls
sections.body:
From the MCP security best practices (2026-07-28 revision):

- **Token passthrough is forbidden:** MCP servers MUST NOT accept tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.
- **Confused deputy:** MCP proxy servers that use a static client ID with a third-party authorization server MUST get per-client consent, use exact redirect URI matching and single-use `state`.
- **SSRF in OAuth metadata discovery:** require HTTPS, block private and link-local ranges such as 169.254.0.0/16, validate redirects, and watch for DNS rebinding.
- **State handle hijacking:** the 2026-07-28 spec is stateless; possessing a state handle is not authentication, so bind handles to the user.
- **Authorization URL validation:** accept only http(s) URLs, reject `javascript:`, and never open URLs through a shell.

keyPoints: Filter retrieval by the user's permissions inside the query; back it with RLS as a non-owner role.
Excessive agency = too much functionality, permission or autonomy; fix each separately.
MCP tool descriptions are untrusted unless the server is trusted; get consent before tool calls.
MCP servers must not accept tokens issued for another audience (no token passthrough).

gotchas.trap: Testing RLS on the chunks table while connected as the owner and seeing all rows "work".
gotchas.correct: Owners and superusers bypass RLS; test as the non-owner app role.

gotchas.trap: Treating a pinned MCP server version as safe by definition.
gotchas.correct: Pinning stops silent changes, not a payload already in the pinned version; review what you pin.

lessons.lab: Create a chunks table with a tenant_id column and an RLS policy. Query it as the owner, then as a new non-owner role, and compare row counts.

lessons.title: Dependencies and build integrity
lessons.summary: How a small team keeps third-party code honest: lockfiles and clean installs, install scripts, typosquatting, update policies with Dependabot, SHA-pinned CI actions, short-lived CI credentials and SLSA build provenance.

sections.heading: Why supply chain is its own category
sections.body:
The OWASP Top 10:2025 adds **A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures**, which widens the 2021 entry on vulnerable and outdated components. It now covers compromised packages, build systems and CI, not just old library versions.

Recent incidents show why this matters:
- **Shai-Hulud npm worm (CISA alert, 2025-09-23):** more than 500 packages were compromised to steal credentials. CISA advised teams to review lockfiles, pin to versions published before 2025-09-16, and rotate credentials.
- **tj-actions/changed-files (CVE-2025-30066):** an attacker repointed the action's existing version tags to a malicious commit, so every workflow that referenced a tag ran the attacker's code and could leak CI secrets into logs.

In both cases nothing was wrong in the victims' own code. The attacker reached them through something they trusted by name.

sections.heading: Lockfiles and reproducible installs
sections.body:
A lockfile records the exact resolved version and integrity hash of every direct and transitive dependency. Commit it, and in CI install from it rather than re-resolving ranges:

```bash
npm ci                          # fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree
yarn install --frozen-lockfile  # Yarn equivalent
```

The OWASP NPM Security Cheat Sheet recommends this because any inconsistency aborts the install instead of quietly pulling a newer, possibly malicious, release. Review lockfile diffs in pull requests. A new transitive package or a changed `resolved` URL deserves the same attention as new code. GitHub **dependency review** shows dependency changes and known vulnerabilities on a pull request, so you can block a risky addition before merging it.

sections.heading: Install scripts, typosquatting and slopsquatting
sections.body:
npm packages can declare lifecycle scripts (`preinstall`, `install`, `postinstall`) that run arbitrary code on the machine that installs them, including CI runners that hold secrets. Worms such as Shai-Hulud spread this way.

- **npm v12 (GA 2026-07-08)** changed the default: dependency lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp builds no longer run unless explicitly allowed (`allowScripts`). Git and remote-URL dependencies are also opt-in. Older npm versions still run scripts by default, so set `ignore-scripts=true` in `.npmrc` and allowlist only the packages that truly need a build step.
- **Typosquatting:** attackers publish packages whose names look like popular ones and wait for a typo.
- **Slopsquatting:** attackers register package names that AI coding assistants tend to hallucinate. The name looks plausible because a model invented it.

Defence for both: check that a package exists, is maintained and is the one you meant before adding it, and never install a name only because an assistant suggested it.

sections.heading: Update policy with Dependabot
sections.body:
Staying current matters, because known-vulnerable versions are the classic supply-chain failure. Updating to a release that is only hours old also carries risk, because many malicious releases are found and pulled within days.

Dependabot gives you two levers:
- **Security updates** open pull requests for dependencies with known advisories. Merge them quickly after CI passes.
- **Version updates** keep you current on a schedule. The `cooldown` option delays version updates for a configurable number of days, set by default or per semver level (`semver-major-days` and so on), with `include` and `exclude` lists. The options reference states that cooldown applies to version updates, not security updates.

A sane small-team policy is: group minor and patch version updates weekly with a cooldown, review majors by hand, and treat security updates as urgent.

sections.heading: Hardening CI: pin actions, scope credentials
sections.body:
A third-party action runs with your workflow's token and secrets. GitHub's secure-use guidance says to **pin actions to a full-length commit SHA**, because a tag can be moved (as happened with tj-actions) but a commit SHA cannot be changed without producing a SHA-1 collision. Since August 2025, an organisation's allowed-actions policy can **require** SHA pinning and **block** specific actions.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read            # least privilege for GITHUB_TOKEN
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-40-char-sha>  # version comment here
```

Other controls from the same guidance:
- Do not combine `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` with a checkout of an untrusted pull request's code.
- Pass untrusted input such as a pull request title through an intermediate environment variable, never by interpolating it straight into a `run:` script.
- Use **OIDC** to get short-lived cloud credentials per job instead of storing long-lived cloud keys as repository secrets. For npm, **trusted publishing** (OIDC) is the recommended way to publish.

sections.heading: Provenance, attestations and SLSA levels
sections.body:
**Provenance** is signed metadata saying which source, build platform and instructions produced an artifact. SLSA v1.2 defines Build track levels:

| Level | Requirement | Protects against |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | none | nothing |
| L1 | provenance exists | mistakes; it is trivial to forge |
| L2 | hosted build platform signs the provenance | tampering after the build |
| L3 | hardened platform: isolated runs, signing secrets unavailable to user steps | tampering during the build |

SLSA v1.2 also adds a Source track alongside the Build track.

GitHub **artifact attestations** by themselves provide SLSA Build Level 2. Building in a shared reusable workflow can provide the isolation needed for Build Level 3. Consumers check an artifact with `gh attestation verify`. Attestations in private repositories use GitHub's own Sigstore instance, which has no public transparency log. Provenance helps only if someone verifies it before deploying.

sections.heading: Runtime seat belts
sections.body: The Node.js Permission Model (`--permission` with `--allow-fs-read`, `--allow-fs-write`, `--allow-child-process` and similar flags) can restrict what a process may touch. The Node docs say plainly that it **does not protect against malicious code**: treat it as a seat belt for mistakes, not as a sandbox for untrusted dependencies. Isolation for code you do not trust comes from containers, separate accounts and network egress limits.

keyPoints: Commit lockfiles and install with npm ci (or a frozen-lockfile flag) in CI so drift aborts the build.
npm v12 no longer runs dependency lifecycle scripts by default. On older npm, set ignore-scripts and allowlist.
Typosquatting exploits typos, while slopsquatting exploits package names that AI assistants hallucinate.
Dependabot security updates should be merged fast. Cooldown delays version updates only.
Pin third-party actions to full-length commit SHAs, keep GITHUB_TOKEN permissions minimal, and prefer OIDC to stored cloud keys.
Artifact attestations give SLSA Build L2. A shared reusable workflow can reach L3. Verify before you deploy.

gotchas.trap: Pinning actions to a version tag such as @v4 is as safe as pinning a SHA.
gotchas.correct: Tags can be repointed, as in the tj-actions compromise. Only a full-length commit SHA is immutable.

gotchas.trap: SLSA Build L1 provenance proves the artifact was not tampered with.
gotchas.correct: L1 provenance is trivial to forge. Tamper resistance starts at L2, where a hosted platform signs it.

gotchas.trap: Running Node with --permission makes it safe to run an untrusted package.
gotchas.correct: The Node docs say the Permission Model does not protect against malicious code.

gotchas.trap: A Dependabot cooldown will delay my security patches.
gotchas.correct: The options reference states that cooldown applies to version updates, not security updates.

lessons.lab: In a sample repo: commit the lockfile and switch CI to npm ci; add ignore-scripts=true to .npmrc and note which packages break; replace every third-party uses: tag with a full SHA plus a version comment; add a top-level permissions: contents: read; add a dependabot.yml with weekly grouped version updates and a cooldown; then add an artifact attestation step and run gh attestation verify on the output.

lessons.title: Cloud, containers, headers and TLS
lessons.summary: The infrastructure basics that stop most real-world exposure: least-privilege IAM with temporary credentials, blocked public buckets, non-root containers, minimal network exposure, and a baseline of security headers and TLS.

sections.heading: IAM: identities, temporary credentials, least privilege
sections.body:
AWS IAM best practices give a short checklist that carries over to any cloud:
- **Humans** sign in through federation with an identity provider and get **temporary credentials**, with MFA required.
- **Workloads** (servers, functions, CI) use **IAM roles** with temporary credentials, not long-lived access keys baked into config. In CI, use OIDC federation.
- Protect the root user and do not use it for daily work.
- **Apply least privilege:** begin from managed policies if needed, then narrow them. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the access a role actually used.
- Regularly remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials.

A wildcard policy (`"Action": "*"`, `"Resource": "*"`) on an application role turns any code-execution or SSRF bug into full account compromise.

sections.heading: Storage that is private by default
sections.body:
Amazon S3 says new buckets, access points and objects **do not allow public access by default**, but people can still change bucket policies or object permissions to make data public. **S3 Block Public Access** settings at the account or bucket level override those policies and ACLs. Keep it on at the account level, and serve public assets through a CDN or a deliberately separate bucket rather than by opening up the data bucket.

Instance metadata is the other classic cloud leak. The OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends **migrating to IMDSv2 and disabling IMDSv1**, so that an SSRF bug cannot simply read role credentials from 169.254.169.254.

sections.heading: Containers: non-root, minimal, no extra privileges
sections.body:
Docker's building best practices say that if a service can run without privileges, use the `USER` instruction to switch to a non-root user that you create in the Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=node:node . .
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

On Kubernetes, the **Restricted** Pod Security Standard requires containers to run as non-root (`runAsNonRoot: true`), to set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, to drop all capabilities, and to use a `RuntimeDefault` (or Localhost) seccomp profile. Use small base images, keep secrets out of image layers, and never mount the Docker socket into an application container.

sections.heading: Network exposure
sections.body: Expose only what users need: the load balancer or CDN on 443. Databases, caches, admin panels and metrics endpoints belong on private networks, reachable through a VPN, bastion or identity-aware proxy. Add egress controls so that a compromised workload cannot reach arbitrary hosts. This is also a network-layer SSRF defence. Debug ports and dashboards bound to 0.0.0.0 are a common way staging environments get breached.

sections.heading: Security headers baseline
sections.body:
A practical header set for an HTML app:

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-RANDOM' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()
```

- **HSTS** is ignored when it arrives over plain HTTP. `max-age=0` turns it off. Preload lists require `max-age` of at least 31536000 (one year) plus `includeSubDomains`, and preload is not part of the HSTS spec. The first visit before a header is seen stays exposed unless the site is preloaded.
- **Referrer-Policy:** the browser default is now `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`. Set it explicitly, or use `no-referrer` on pages whose URLs carry sensitive data.
- **Permissions-Policy:** an empty allowlist `()` disables a feature in the page and in all nested frames. `*` allows it everywhere.
- **X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff** stops MIME sniffing, together with correct `Content-Type` values.
- **frame-ancestors** in CSP replaces X-Frame-Options for clickjacking defence. `upgrade-insecure-requests` does not replace HSTS.

sections.heading: Cookies and TLS
sections.body:
Session cookies should be `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, preferably with the `__Host-` prefix (requires Secure, no Domain, `Path=/`). `SameSite=None` requires `Secure`.

For TLS, the OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet says web applications must default to **TLS 1.3** and may support **TLS 1.2** for compatibility. **TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and must be disabled.** Automate certificate renewal so that an expired certificate never becomes an outage, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS before HSTS takes over.

keyPoints: Humans federate, workloads assume roles: temporary credentials everywhere, with least privilege refined from real usage.
Keep S3 Block Public Access on at the account level. Use IMDSv2 only.
Containers run as a non-root USER. Kubernetes Restricted requires runAsNonRoot and no privilege escalation.
Expose only the edge. Data stores and admin tools stay private, with egress limited.
HSTS is ignored over HTTP, and preloading needs max-age of at least one year plus includeSubDomains.
Permissions-Policy feature=() disables a feature. TLS 1.3 is the default, 1.2 is allowed, and 1.0/1.1 are disabled.

gotchas.trap: Sending HSTS on the HTTP response protects users from the first request.
gotchas.correct: Browsers ignore HSTS received over HTTP. Only HTTPS responses or the preload list count.

gotchas.trap: upgrade-insecure-requests in CSP is a substitute for HSTS.
gotchas.correct: It rewrites subresource URLs. It does not replace HSTS.

gotchas.trap: S3 buckets are private by default, so Block Public Access is redundant.
gotchas.correct: Defaults can be changed by a policy or ACL edit. Block Public Access overrides those changes.

gotchas.trap: A container running as root is fine because it is isolated.
gotchas.correct: Docker docs say to switch to a non-root USER when the service does not need privileges, which limits the impact of an escape or RCE.

lessons.lab: Take a small app and: rebuild its image with a non-root USER and confirm with docker run ... id; add the header baseline above and check it in browser devtools; set Permissions-Policy to disable camera, microphone and geolocation; check the TLS listener rejects TLS 1.1; and in a cloud sandbox enable account-level S3 Block Public Access and require IMDSv2 on a test instance.

lessons.title: Incident response for a small team
lessons.summary: A lightweight incident process for a small product team: prepare, detect, contain, rotate, notify on legal deadlines, recover, and learn through a blameless postmortem.

sections.heading: The framework: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3
sections.body:
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) supersedes Rev. 2. Instead of the old four-phase lifecycle (preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity), it is a **CSF 2.0 Community Profile**. Incident response is spread across the CSF Functions **Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover**.

The practical point for a small team: most of the work happens *before* the incident. Know who decides, keep the logs you will need, have a list of credentials and how to rotate each one, and know who to contact (cloud provider, lawyer, data protection officer).

sections.heading: Running the incident
sections.body:
Google's SRE book recommends declaring incidents early and separating roles so the person fixing things is not also fielding questions:
- **Incident commander:** owns the overall response and makes the calls.
- **Operations:** the people making changes to systems.
- **Communications:** updates stakeholders and customers on a schedule.
- **Planning:** handles longer-term work such as filing bugs and arranging handoffs.
- A **living incident document**, kept by the incident commander, records the timeline and decisions as they happen.

On a team of three, one person can hold two roles, but say out loud who is commanding.

sections.heading: Contain, then rotate
sections.body:
Containment stops further damage while you preserve evidence. Examples: disable the compromised key, block the malicious IP or token, take the vulnerable endpoint offline, or revoke a compromised deploy pipeline's credentials. Snapshot disks and logs before you wipe anything.

For leaked secrets, GitHub's secret scanning guidance is blunt: **rotate the affected credential immediately**. Rewriting Git history is often unnecessary if the credential has already been revoked, because the value is now useless. Rotation must also cover everything the attacker could have reached: after a CI compromise such as tj-actions or Shai-Hulud, treat every secret that job could read as exposed, including cloud keys, npm tokens and the GITHUB_TOKEN's downstream effects.

sections.heading: Notification duties
sections.body:
Deadlines are set in law, and the clock often starts earlier than teams expect.
- **GDPR Article 33:** a controller notifies the supervisory authority **without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware** of a personal-data breach, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. A late notification must explain the delay. Information can be provided in phases. A **processor** must notify its controller without undue delay. Article 34 separately covers telling the affected people when the risk to them is high.
- **US public companies:** SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 is due **four business days after the company determines the incident is material**, not four days after discovery.
- **CIRCIA** (US critical infrastructure): as of late 2026 the final rule has not been issued, so its proposed 72-hour and 24-hour deadlines are not yet mandatory.
- **US state breach laws** vary by state. Do not assume one number.

Bring in legal counsel early. Engineers supply facts and timelines, and lawyers decide on notifications.

sections.heading: Recover and learn: the blameless postmortem
sections.body:
Recovery means restoring from known-good builds and credentials, then watching closely for the attacker's return. Afterwards, write a postmortem. The SRE book defines it as **blameless**: it focuses on contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team". Blame teaches people to hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes come back as the next incident.

A good postmortem includes impact, a timeline, root and contributing causes, what went well, and **owned, dated action items** such as "require SHA pinning across the org" or "move CI to OIDC". The postmortem is shared openly so others can learn from it.

keyPoints: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 maps incident response onto CSF 2.0 Functions and supersedes the four-phase Rev. 2 model.
Declare early, name an incident commander, and keep a live incident document.
Contain first and preserve evidence. Rotate leaked secrets immediately, because revocation matters more than history rewrites.
GDPR: notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, where feasible. SEC 8-K: 4 business days after determining materiality.
CIRCIA reporting deadlines are still proposals. US state laws vary.
Postmortems are blameless and end in owned, dated action items.

gotchas.trap: The GDPR 72-hour clock starts when the investigation is complete.
gotchas.correct: It starts on becoming aware of the breach. Details may follow in phases.

gotchas.trap: Force-pushing to remove a leaked key from Git history fixes the leak.
gotchas.correct: Rotate the credential immediately. Once it is revoked, rewriting history is often unnecessary.

gotchas.trap: SEC Item 1.05 requires filing within four business days of discovering the incident.
gotchas.correct: The four business days run from the determination that the incident is material.

gotchas.trap: A postmortem should identify who made the mistake.
gotchas.correct: Blameless postmortems focus on contributing causes without indicting individuals.

lessons.lab: Write a one-page incident runbook for your app: roles, the chat channel and incident-document template, a table of every credential with its owner and rotation steps, the regulators and contacts with their deadlines, and a postmortem template. Then run a 30-minute tabletop: "a CI action we use was compromised two days ago".

flashcards.front: What are the four key questions of threat modelling?
flashcards.back: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job?

flashcards.front: What five element types appear in a data-flow diagram for threat modelling?
flashcards.back: External entities, processes, data stores, data flows and trust boundaries.

flashcards.front: What is a trust boundary?
flashcards.back: A line where data or control passes between parties with different levels of trust. Every flow crossing it must be authenticated, validated and authorised.

flashcards.front: What does STRIDE stand for?
flashcards.back: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

flashcards.front: Which security property does each STRIDE category violate?
flashcards.back: Spoofing: authentication. Tampering: integrity. Repudiation: accounting (non-repudiation). Information disclosure: confidentiality. Denial of service: availability. Elevation of privilege: authorisation.

flashcards.front: How does the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet say threats should be ranked?
flashcards.back: In theory by the product of likelihood and impact; in practice that is hard to compute and ignores fix effort, so a coarse grid is fine and some practitioners also weigh the effort of the fix.

flashcards.front: What are the four responses to an identified threat?
flashcards.back: Mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept. Transfer does not reduce the harm itself; document who owns the residual risk.

flashcards.front: What design lesson does CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js middleware bypass) teach?
flashcards.back: Never enforce authorisation only in middleware or one edge layer. Re-check in the handler or data layer, and patch the framework.

flashcards.front: What does "deny by default" mean for application routes?
flashcards.back: A route requires authentication and an explicit permission unless deliberately marked public, so a forgotten annotation fails closed.

flashcards.front: Which Postgres roles bypass row-level security?
flashcards.back: Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS and, normally, the table owner. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes the owner subject to policies.

flashcards.front: What happens when RLS is enabled on a Postgres table but no policy exists?
flashcards.back: Access is default deny: no rows are visible or modifiable by roles subject to RLS.

flashcards.front: What credentials should cloud workloads use per AWS IAM best practices?
flashcards.back: IAM roles with temporary credentials, not long-lived access keys, with least-privilege policies.

flashcards.front: What is the latest stable OWASP ASVS version and its shape?
flashcards.back: ASVS 5.0.0 (30 May 2025): 17 chapters and 345 requirements, 70 of them (about 20%) at Level 1.

flashcards.front: ASVS levels: where should a small team start?
flashcards.back: Meet Level 1 (first-layer defences) for every app first, then Level 2 for apps handling sensitive data. Level 3 adds the most depth and is for the highest-risk systems.

flashcards.front: How should ASVS requirements be referenced, and why?
flashcards.back: With the version prefix, for example v5.0.0-1.2.5, because identifiers change between versions; 4.0.3 numbers do not carry over to 5.0.

flashcards.front: Which events must always be logged for security?
flashcards.back: Authentication successes and failures, authorisation failures, input validation and session failures, and high-risk or admin actions.

flashcards.front: Name data that should never be written directly to logs.
flashcards.back: Passwords, access tokens, session IDs, connection strings, encryption keys, payment card data and sensitive PII. Mask, hash or remove them.

flashcards.front: How do you prevent log injection?
flashcards.back: Sanitise CR, LF and delimiter characters and use structured logging with a correct encoder; parameterised messages alone do not stop CR/LF injection.

flashcards.front: What is A09 in the OWASP Top 10:2025?
flashcards.back: Security Logging & Alerting Failures, renamed from "Logging and Monitoring" to emphasise the alerting needed to act on logged events.

flashcards.front: What is GitHub's first step when a secret is committed?
flashcards.back: Rotate the affected credential immediately. Rewriting history is often unnecessary once it is revoked.

flashcards.front: Which push-protection bypass reason leaves an open alert?
flashcards.back: "I'll fix it later" creates an open alert. "Used in tests" and "false positive" create closed alerts.

flashcards.front: How do you add SAST to a legacy repo without drowning in noise?
flashcards.back: Baseline and triage existing alerts once, gate pull requests only on new high-severity findings, and burn down the backlog on a schedule.

flashcards.front: Minimum password length under NIST SP 800-63B-4 when the password is the only factor?
flashcards.back: 15 characters. A password used only as part of MFA can be as short as 8. Verifiers SHOULD allow at least 64.

flashcards.front: Does 800-63B-4 allow composition rules such as "one uppercase, one symbol"?
flashcards.back: No. Composition rules SHALL NOT be imposed. Use length plus a blocklist check instead.

flashcards.front: When does 800-63B-4 allow forcing a password change?
flashcards.back: Only on evidence of compromise. Periodic forced changes SHALL NOT be required.

flashcards.front: What must a verifier check a new password against?
flashcards.back: A blocklist of breached passwords, dictionary words and context-specific words, checking the whole password. If it rejects one, it must tell the user why.

flashcards.front: Failed-attempt limit in 800-63B-4?
flashcards.back: No more than 100 consecutive failed attempts per authenticator. Add IP and global rate limits on top.

flashcards.front: OWASP minimum Argon2id parameters?
flashcards.back: m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1. Equivalent trade-offs include m=46 MiB with t=1.

flashcards.front: bcrypt input limit, and its OWASP status?
flashcards.back: 72 bytes. OWASP lists bcrypt (work factor at least 10) for legacy systems only.

flashcards.front: PBKDF2 setting when FIPS compliance is required?
flashcards.back: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations (or HMAC-SHA-512 with 220,000).

flashcards.front: What is a pepper, and where does it live?
flashcards.back: A secret key applied as an extra keyed hashing step. It is stored apart from the password database, for example in an HSM, TEE or TPM, as NIST SP 800-63B-4 suggests.

flashcards.front: Can synced passkeys be used at NIST AAL3?
flashcards.back: No. Syncable authenticators are allowed at AAL1 and AAL2 but SHALL NOT be used at AAL3.

flashcards.front: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
flashcards.back: The credential is scoped to the relying party ID and the authenticator signs a fresh challenge, so a look-alike domain cannot obtain a usable assertion.

flashcards.front: Status of email as an out-of-band authenticator in 800-63B-4?
flashcards.back: Email SHALL NOT be used for out-of-band authentication. SMS and voice are restricted and need an offered alternative.

flashcards.front: Minimum entropy for a session ID (OWASP)?
flashcards.back: At least 64 bits from a CSPRNG, for example at least 16 hex characters.

flashcards.front: What does the __Host- cookie prefix require?
flashcards.back: Secure, no Domain attribute, and Path=/. This locks the cookie to the exact host.

flashcards.front: What do the __Http- and __Host-Http- prefixes add?
flashcards.back: They also require HttpOnly, which proves the cookie was set by a Set-Cookie header and not by script.

flashcards.front: Does HttpOnly stop CSRF?
flashcards.back: No. It stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, but the browser still sends the cookie with requests, including fetch and XHR.

flashcards.front: What does SameSite=None require?
flashcards.back: The Secure attribute. Without it, browsers reject the cookie.

flashcards.front: When must a session ID be regenerated?
flashcards.back: After login and after any privilege change. This defeats session fixation.

flashcards.front: What must logout do on the server?
flashcards.back: Invalidate the session on the server. Clearing the browser cookie alone leaves stolen copies valid.

flashcards.front: Which PKCE challenge method is acceptable per RFC 9700?
flashcards.back: S256 only. Public clients MUST use PKCE.

flashcards.front: Which OAuth grants does RFC 9700 rule out?
flashcards.back: Implicit SHOULD NOT be used. Resource owner password credentials MUST NOT be used.

flashcards.front: How must an authorization server match redirect URIs?
flashcards.back: By exact string comparison. Only the loopback port may vary for native apps.

flashcards.front: Difference between OAuth state and the OIDC nonce?
flashcards.back: state is checked on the callback to stop CSRF. nonce is checked inside the ID token to stop token replay.

flashcards.front: What does RFC 9207 iss checking defend against?
flashcards.back: Mix-up attacks, where a client using several authorization servers is tricked into sending a code to the wrong one.

flashcards.front: Which browser-app pattern does RFC 10017 strongly recommend for sensitive data?
flashcards.back: Backend for frontend (BFF): tokens stay on the server, and the browser holds a Secure, HttpOnly __Host-Http- session cookie.

flashcards.front: What is JWT algorithm confusion?
flashcards.back: The verifier trusts the alg header, so an attacker switches RS256 to HS256 and signs with the public key as the HMAC secret. To prevent it, pin the accepted algorithms.

flashcards.front: Which JWT claims must be validated beyond the signature?
flashcards.back: iss (expected issuer), aud (this service), and exp and nbf (time), with small clock skew.

flashcards.front: How can you revoke JWT access tokens before they expire?
flashcards.back: Use short lifetimes with rotated, revocable refresh tokens. Add a jti denylist or token introspection for urgent cases.

flashcards.front: Where does Broken Access Control rank in the OWASP Top 10:2025, and what was folded into it?
flashcards.back: A01:2025, still first. SSRF is now part of A01.

flashcards.front: What CWE is the classic IDOR, and where does Missing Authorization rank in the 2025 CWE Top 25?
flashcards.back: IDOR is CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (#24). CWE-862 Missing Authorization is #4.

flashcards.front: BOLA vs BFLA?
flashcards.back: BOLA (API1:2023): caller reaches an object they should not. BFLA (API5:2023): caller invokes a function or operation, such as an admin action, they should not.

flashcards.front: Do unguessable UUIDs fix IDOR?
flashcards.back: No. They are defence in depth. The server must check access to the specific object on every request.

flashcards.front: Where should a multi-tenant app get the current tenant id?
flashcards.back: From the authenticated session or token, never from a client-controlled header, query parameter or body.

flashcards.front: Lesson from CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js middleware bypass)?
flashcards.back: Do not enforce authorization only in middleware; re-check in the handler or data layer.

flashcards.front: RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC?
flashcards.back: RBAC: permissions via roles. ABAC: policy over subject, object, action and context attributes. ReBAC: access follows relationships in a graph (Zanzibar-style), good for sharing and inheritance.

flashcards.front: PostgreSQL: RLS is enabled on a table but no policy exists. What can a normal role see?
flashcards.back: Nothing. RLS with no policy is default-deny.

flashcards.front: Who bypasses PostgreSQL row-level security?
flashcards.back: Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS and, unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, the table owner.

flashcards.front: RLS: USING vs WITH CHECK?
flashcards.back: USING filters rows read or targeted by UPDATE/DELETE. WITH CHECK validates rows written; if omitted it defaults to the USING expression.

flashcards.front: RLS: how do permissive and restrictive policies combine?
flashcards.back: Permissive policies are OR-ed; restrictive policies are AND-ed with the result. Use AS RESTRICTIVE for tenant isolation.

flashcards.front: How do you set a per-request tenant setting safely with pooled connections?
flashcards.back: `SET LOCAL` (or `set_config(name, value, true)`) inside the request transaction, so it resets at commit or rollback.

flashcards.front: Why can a PostgreSQL view leak rows past RLS, and what fixes it?
flashcards.back: By default a view accesses tables with the view owner's privileges. Create it WITH (security_invoker = true) to check the calling user.

flashcards.front: Envelope encryption in one line?
flashcards.back: A DEK encrypts the data; a KMS-held KEK encrypts the DEK; the wrapped DEK is stored with the ciphertext.

flashcards.front: What does disk or storage encryption at rest protect against, and what not?
flashcards.back: Lost or stolen media and copied snapshots. Not queries through the app, stolen DB credentials or SQL injection.

flashcards.front: Hash or encrypt: user passwords, issued API keys, a customer's third-party API secret?
flashcards.back: Hash passwords (slow password hash) and issued API keys; encrypt the third-party secret because the app must reuse it.

flashcards.front: A secret was pushed to a public repo. First action?
flashcards.back: Revoke or rotate it at the provider immediately. GitHub notes history rewriting is often unnecessary once revoked.

flashcards.front: Why not pass a token as a Docker build ARG?
flashcards.back: Build args and ENV persist in the image and its metadata. Use `RUN --mount=type=secret`.

flashcards.front: Push protection bypass reasons and resulting alert state?
flashcards.back: "Used in tests" or "false positive" create a closed alert; "I'll fix it later" creates an open alert.

flashcards.front: What do you need for secret scanning on private organization repositories on GitHub?
flashcards.back: GitHub Secret Protection (Team or Enterprise Cloud). It is free on public repositories.

flashcards.front: Why are short-lived credentials better than stored access keys in CI?
flashcards.back: They expire on their own and nothing long-lived is stored to leak; OIDC federation lets CI assume a scoped role without any stored cloud key.

flashcards.front: GDPR Article 33 deadline?
flashcards.back: Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware; explain any delay; phased information is allowed.

flashcards.front: Which GDPR Article 5 principles map to "collect less" and "keep it less long"?
flashcards.back: Data minimisation and storage limitation.

flashcards.front: What belongs in an audit trail entry?
flashcards.back: Who (actor id), what (action, target id), when, from where, outcome. Append-only for the app, without secrets or raw sensitive values.

flashcards.front: Why is an ORM not automatic protection against SQL injection?
flashcards.back: ORMs parameterize the queries they generate, but raw query methods and raw fragments (where, orderBy) built by string concatenation are just as injectable as hand-written SQL.

flashcards.front: Can you bind a column name or sort direction as a query parameter?
flashcards.back: No. Parameters bind values, not identifiers or keywords. Map user input to a hardcoded allowlist of column names and ASC/DESC in code.

flashcards.front: Are stored procedures always safe from SQL injection?
flashcards.back: No. They are only safe if they do not build dynamic SQL from their inputs inside the procedure.

flashcards.front: What is NoSQL operator injection and the main defense?
flashcards.back: A parser turns attacker input into an object holding a query operator instead of a plain value. Validate the type and shape of every input with a schema before it reaches a query.

flashcards.front: Node.js: exec versus execFile for running a program with user input?
flashcards.back: exec runs the command through a shell, so metacharacters are interpreted. execFile and spawn (without shell: true) pass an argument array with no shell.

flashcards.front: What is argument (option) injection?
flashcards.back: Even without a shell, a value starting with a dash can be read as an option by the target program. Validate against a strict pattern and put -- before user positional arguments where supported.

flashcards.front: Name the main XSS output contexts.
flashcards.back: HTML body, quoted HTML attribute, JavaScript, CSS and URL. Each needs its own encoding or handling; HTML encoding alone is not safe in script or URL contexts.

flashcards.front: How do you safely put a user value in a URL parameter inside an href?
flashcards.back: Percent-encode the parameter value, then attribute-encode the whole attribute. For full user URLs, validate the scheme (allow https, reject javascript:).

flashcards.front: What is the key rule when sanitizing user HTML with DOMPurify?
flashcards.back: Sanitize the final HTML immediately before insertion and do not modify it afterwards, because post-processing can reintroduce dangerous markup.

flashcards.front: textContent or innerHTML for displaying user text in the DOM?
flashcards.back: textContent. It treats the value as text, so markup is never parsed.

flashcards.front: Name three framework XSS escape hatches.
flashcards.back: React dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Angular bypassSecurityTrustAs* methods, and Lit unsafeHTML. Each disables the framework's default escaping.

flashcards.front: What does a strict CSP contain, per MDN?
flashcards.back: A nonce- or hash-based script-src, plus object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' (often with 'strict-dynamic').

flashcards.front: When should you use a CSP hash instead of a nonce?
flashcards.back: For static or cached HTML. A nonce must be unique per response, so it cannot be baked into static pages.

flashcards.front: What happens to 'unsafe-inline' when a nonce or hash is present in script-src?
flashcards.back: Browsers ignore it. It can stay only as a fallback for very old browsers. 'unsafe-eval' is not ignored.

flashcards.front: What does 'strict-dynamic' do?
flashcards.back: It extends trust from a nonced or hashed script to the scripts that script loads, so you do not need long host allowlists.

flashcards.front: report-uri or report-to for CSP reporting?
flashcards.back: report-to with a Reporting-Endpoints header is recommended; report-uri is deprecated. Sending both covers older browsers for now.

flashcards.front: Can Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only be set with a meta tag?
flashcards.back: No. It must be sent as an HTTP response header.

flashcards.front: Which CSP directive enforces Trusted Types for DOM XSS sinks?
flashcards.back: require-trusted-types-for 'script'.

flashcards.front: Does upgrade-insecure-requests replace HSTS?
flashcards.back: No. It tells the browser to upgrade the page's insecure (http) request URLs to https. HSTS tells the browser to use HTTPS for every future request to the host, including http:// links and typed addresses.

flashcards.front: What role does SameSite play in CSRF defense, per OWASP?
flashcards.back: Defense in depth only. It "does not replace a proper CSRF defense", and Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations.

flashcards.front: Naive versus signed double-submit cookie?
flashcards.back: Naive double-submit (random cookie echoed in a field) is discouraged. The signed variant binds the token to the session with an HMAC.

flashcards.front: How does Fetch Metadata defend against CSRF?
flashcards.back: The server rejects state-changing requests whose Sec-Fetch-Site shows a cross-site origin, falling back to Origin/Referer checks when the header is absent. OWASP lists it as a primary option for modern-browser apps.

flashcards.front: What is login CSRF and how is it defended?
flashcards.back: An attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account so their activity is captured. Defend with CSRF tokens tied to a pre-session created before login.

flashcards.front: Can Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * be used with credentialed requests?
flashcards.back: No, browsers reject the wildcard for credentialed requests. Reflecting any Origin with credentials is the dangerous workaround to avoid.

flashcards.front: Why should you not allow the null origin in CORS?
flashcards.back: Sandboxed documents and data: or file: resources send Origin: null, so an attacker can produce it. MDN says null should not be used.

flashcards.front: What replaces X-Frame-Options for clickjacking defense?
flashcards.back: The CSP frame-ancestors directive ('none' or 'self'), sent as a response header. Sending both covers older browsers.

flashcards.front: How does IMDSv2 reduce SSRF impact on EC2?
flashcards.back: It requires a session token obtained with a PUT request and sent on each call, which a simple SSRF GET cannot obtain. Require IMDSv2 and disable IMDSv1.

flashcards.front: Why does a hostname allowlist alone not stop SSRF?
flashcards.back: DNS rebinding: the name can resolve to a safe IP at check time and an internal IP when the client connects. Resolve, validate, then connect to the validated IP.

flashcards.front: How do you check that a resolved file path stays in the base directory?
flashcards.back: Canonicalize to an absolute path and check it starts with the base directory plus a path separator; better still, use server-generated file IDs.

flashcards.front: What does the Python documentation say about pickle?
flashcards.back: The pickle module is not secure; only unpickle data you trust. Use JSON with schema validation for untrusted input.

flashcards.front: Why are SVG uploads risky?
flashcards.back: SVG can contain script, so serving user SVGs inline from your main origin can cause stored XSS. Serve from a separate domain or as attachments, or convert them.

flashcards.front: Where do XSS, SQL injection and path traversal rank in the 2025 CWE Top 25?
flashcards.back: CWE-79 (XSS) is #1, CWE-89 (SQL injection) is #2 and CWE-22 (path traversal) is #6.

flashcards.front: Name the ten OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 risks in order.
flashcards.back: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (all :2025).

flashcards.front: Why must you always write the year suffix on LLM Top 10 IDs?
flashcards.back: The 2026 edition (August 2026) renumbers the list. For example, Improper Output Handling is LLM05:2025 but LLM10:2026, and Excessive Agency is LLM06:2025 but LLM03:2026.

flashcards.front: What replaced System Prompt Leakage in the 2026 LLM Top 10?
flashcards.back: LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure, which broadens it to everything in the model's hidden context.

flashcards.front: Direct vs indirect prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Direct: the user types the malicious instructions. Indirect: the instructions arrive in third-party content the model reads (web pages, emails, files, tool results), and the user is the victim.

flashcards.front: Why can prompt injection not be fully filtered?
flashcards.back: LLMs make no architectural distinction between instructions and data, so there is no equivalent of parameterized queries. OWASP states no reliable prevention mechanism exists today.

flashcards.front: The "Rule of Two" (OWASP 2026 prompt injection guidance)
flashcards.back: Avoid combining untrusted input, sensitive data, and state change or external communication in one flow without human oversight. Remove one leg or add approval.

flashcards.front: Where does Anthropic say untrusted content should go in a Claude request?
flashcards.back: Only in `tool_result` blocks, labelled with its source and JSON-encoded, never in the `system` prompt. Your own instructions go in a following user turn, not inside the tool result.

flashcards.front: OpenAI's rule for untrusted variables in agent prompts
flashcards.back: Do not use untrusted variables in developer messages; pass them in user messages. Design workflows so untrusted data never directly drives agent behaviour.

flashcards.front: How do structured outputs reduce prompt injection risk between agent steps?
flashcards.back: Enums and fixed fields validated in code remove free-form channels an attacker could use to pass instructions to the next step.

flashcards.front: Which actions should require human approval in an agent?
flashcards.back: Privileged, irreversible or externally visible actions: payments, deletions, sending email or messages, publishing, permission changes.

flashcards.front: Name three hiding places for indirect prompt injection payloads.
flashcards.back: Any three of: white-on-white or tiny text, HTML comments, invisible Unicode (tag-block or zero-width characters), image alt text, document metadata.

flashcards.front: Can a system prompt safely hold an API key if it says "never reveal this"?
flashcards.back: No. Assume users can see anything the model can see. Keep credentials in server-side tool code and enforce authorization outside the LLM.

flashcards.front: What should never appear in LLM app logs?
flashcards.back: Secrets, session IDs, tokens, and full prompts or completions containing PII unless redacted. Prompt logs are sensitive data with retention and access limits.

flashcards.front: Where must RAG enforce document permissions?
flashcards.back: At retrieval time, inside the vector query (by ACL or tenant), before chunks reach the model. Not by asking the model to withhold content.

flashcards.front: Which 2025 risk covers RAG stores ignoring permissions?
flashcards.back: LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses.

flashcards.front: Who bypasses Postgres row-level security?
flashcards.back: Superusers and table owners (owners unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; superusers always). The app must connect as a non-owner role.

flashcards.front: LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling in one line
flashcards.back: Model output is passed to a browser, shell, interpreter, SQL or API without validation, sanitisation or encoding. Treat output as untrusted user input.

flashcards.front: How can a Markdown image leak chat data?
flashcards.back: An injected answer includes an image whose URL embeds conversation data; the browser fetches it automatically, sending the data to the attacker. Control image and link hosts (allowlist, proxy, CSP img-src).

flashcards.front: Safer alternative to letting the model write free-form SQL
flashcards.back: Have the model pick a predefined parameterized query (an enum) and supply typed parameters. If free SQL is unavoidable: read-only, RLS-restricted, non-owner role with timeouts and row limits.

flashcards.front: Where does a tool handler get the user identity from?
flashcards.back: The authenticated session, never a model-supplied argument such as `user_id`. Then it checks authorization for that user and resource.

flashcards.front: Three roots of LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
flashcards.back: Excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

flashcards.front: How does the MCP spec treat tool descriptions and annotations?
flashcards.back: As untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. Tools are arbitrary code execution, and hosts must get user consent before invoking any tool.

flashcards.front: MCP token passthrough rule
flashcards.back: MCP servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.

flashcards.front: Does pinning an MCP server version make it safe?
flashcards.back: No. Pinning stops silent updates, but it does not stop a payload shipped in the pinned version. Review what you pin.

flashcards.front: OWASP agentic list IDs and two examples
flashcards.back: Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 uses ASI01-ASI10, for example ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack and ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning.

flashcards.front: What does `npm ci` do differently from `npm install`?
flashcards.back: It installs exactly what the lockfile specifies and aborts if package.json and the lockfile disagree, so CI cannot silently pick up a new release.

flashcards.front: What changed about install scripts in npm v12?
flashcards.back: Since npm v12 (GA July 2026), dependency lifecycle scripts (preinstall, install, postinstall) and implicit node-gyp builds do not run unless explicitly allowed (allowScripts).

flashcards.front: Typosquatting vs slopsquatting?
flashcards.back: Typosquatting registers look-alike names to catch human typos. Slopsquatting registers names that AI coding assistants hallucinate, so the suggested package looks legitimate.

flashcards.front: Does a Dependabot cooldown apply to security updates?
flashcards.back: No. The options reference says cooldown is only available for version updates, not security updates.

flashcards.front: Why pin a GitHub Action to a full-length commit SHA instead of a tag?
flashcards.back: Tags can be moved to a malicious commit (as in tj-actions/changed-files, CVE-2025-30066). A commit SHA cannot change without a SHA-1 collision.

flashcards.front: What org-level control did GitHub add in August 2025 for actions?
flashcards.back: The allowed-actions policy can require full-length SHA pinning and block specific actions with a "!" prefix.

flashcards.front: SLSA Build L1 vs L2 vs L3?
flashcards.back: L1: provenance exists (easy to forge). L2: a hosted platform signs provenance (protects after the build). L3: hardened, isolated builds with signing secrets hidden from user steps (protects during the build).

flashcards.front: What SLSA level do GitHub artifact attestations give on their own?
flashcards.back: SLSA Build Level 2. Building in a shared reusable workflow can provide the isolation needed for Build Level 3.

flashcards.front: How do you check an artifact attestation from GitHub?
flashcards.back: Run `gh attestation verify` against the artifact before you deploy or consume it.

flashcards.front: Why use OIDC in CI instead of stored cloud keys?
flashcards.back: Each job gets a short-lived, scoped token from the cloud provider through a trust relationship, so no long-lived cloud secret sits in the repository.

flashcards.front: Is the Node.js Permission Model a sandbox for untrusted packages?
flashcards.back: No. The Node docs say it does not protect against malicious code. It is a seat belt for mistakes.

flashcards.front: AWS IAM: how should humans and workloads get credentials?
flashcards.back: Humans federate through an identity provider and get temporary credentials with MFA. Workloads use IAM roles with temporary credentials, not long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does S3 Block Public Access add if buckets are private by default?
flashcards.back: It overrides bucket policies, access point policies and ACLs that would make data public, so one mistaken edit cannot expose the bucket.

flashcards.front: Which Kubernetes Pod Security Standard requires non-root containers?
flashcards.back: Restricted: it requires runAsNonRoot true, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, dropping all capabilities and a RuntimeDefault or Localhost seccomp profile, among other controls.

flashcards.front: HSTS preload requirements?
flashcards.back: max-age of at least 31536000 (one year) plus includeSubDomains (and the preload token). Preload is not part of the HSTS spec, and HSTS sent over HTTP is ignored.

flashcards.front: What does `Permissions-Policy: camera=()` mean?
flashcards.back: The empty allowlist disables the camera feature in the top-level page and in all nested frames.

flashcards.front: Which TLS versions should a web app accept today?
flashcards.back: Default to TLS 1.3, optionally allow TLS 1.2 for compatibility. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and must be disabled.

flashcards.front: GDPR Art. 33 deadline?
flashcards.back: Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware. Explain any delay, and give details in phases if needed.

flashcards.front: When is an SEC 8-K Item 1.05 filing due?
flashcards.back: Four business days after the company determines the cybersecurity incident is material, not after discovery.

flashcards.front: What makes a postmortem "blameless"?
flashcards.back: It identifies contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, so people report problems honestly. It ends in owned action items.

questions.scenario: First threat model
questions.stem: A four-person team is about to add file uploads and a payment-provider webhook to its SaaS app. They have never threat modelled before and have one afternoon. What should they do first?
options: Run every available scanner against the current codebase and fix the results
Draw a data-flow diagram of the new feature with its external entities, processes, data stores, flows and trust boundaries
Book an external penetration test for after the feature ships
Copy the CWE Top 25 into a checklist and tick off each item
questions.explanation: The first threat-modelling question is "what are we working on", and a data-flow diagram that shows trust boundaries is the most common way to answer it. Threats are then identified against that model. Scanners, generic checklists and later pentests do not tell the team where the new feature crosses trust boundaries.
rationales: Scanners find implementation bugs in existing code, not design threats in a feature not yet built.
Correct. Modelling the system and its trust boundaries is the foundation for finding threats.

questions.scenario: Price field
questions.stem: During a STRIDE session, a developer notes that a user could intercept their own checkout request and change the price field before it reaches the API. Which STRIDE category is this?

Repudiation
Information disclosure
Tampering
