rationales: Spoofing is pretending to be another identity, which is not happening here.
Repudiation is denying an action without the ability to prove otherwise.
Nothing confidential is exposed; the data is altered.

Elevation of privilege; remove the admin role from support staff
Repudiation; record admin actions in a protected audit log with who, what, when and outcome
Information disclosure; encrypt the customer table at rest

C, because it is the quickest fix
A, because it is both easy to exploit and exposes other customers' financial data

Speed of fix matters, but the impact of C is small compared with A.

questions.stem: A team's DFD shows the payment provider sending webhooks to /api/payments/webhook. A developer argues that because the provider is a trusted partner, the handler can mark orders paid directly from the payload. How should the threat model treat this flow?

As out of scope, because third-party systems are the provider's responsibility
As crossing a trust boundary: authenticate the sender and validate the payload before acting on it

questions.scenario: RLS returns everything
questions.stem: A team enabled row-level security on a multi-tenant orders table with a correct tenant policy. In staging, every tenant still sees every row. The application connects as the role that ran the migrations and owns the table. What is the best fix?
options: Add a second, identical permissive policy so the filter applies twice
Grant the application role BYPASSRLS so policies are evaluated consistently
Disable RLS and add WHERE tenant_id clauses in the ORM
Have the application connect as a separate non-owner role with only the grants it needs, and keep the owner for migrations
questions.explanation: Per the PostgreSQL docs, table owners normally bypass RLS (as do superusers and BYPASSRLS roles). Connecting as a restricted runtime role makes the policy apply and also follows least privilege. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is an alternative for owners, but separating roles is the cleaner design.
rationales: Permissive policies are OR-ed, and the owner bypasses them anyway.
BYPASSRLS does exactly what its name says and makes isolation impossible.
This drops the database-level safety net and relies on every query being written correctly.
Correct. A non-owner runtime role is subject to the policy and has minimal privileges.

questions.stem: In a team's framework, every route is public unless a developer adds an @RequireRole annotation. Twice this year a new admin endpoint shipped without it. Which design change addresses the root cause?

Make routes require authentication and an explicit permission by default, with an explicit @Public marker for the few open routes
Move admin endpoints to a URL path that is harder to guess
Log every call to admin endpoints and review the logs weekly

Adopt Level 1 as the baseline for the app, then work toward Level 2 for the chapters that match its sensitive-data risks
Skip ASVS and rely on an annual penetration test
Pick 20 requirements at random from across all three levels

Random selection ignores the levels' risk ordering.

Ask which version is meant, match by requirement text rather than number, and cite requirements in v5.0.0-x.y.z form going forward
Reply that ASVS numbers never change, so the customer has made a typo
Ignore the item because it predates 5.0

questions.stem: An attacker registers the username "alice\n2026-11-12 10:00 INFO admin login success user=root". The app writes usernames into plain-text log lines, and the forged line appears as a separate entry. Which fix is most robust?

Reject usernames longer than 32 characters
Store logs on a separate server so the attacker cannot edit them
Emit structured logs with an encoder that escapes values, and sanitise CR, LF and delimiter characters in event data

Encrypt the log file and keep logging everything
Log metadata such as user, model, token counts and tool calls, with redacted or sampled content held under tighter access and retention

questions.stem: Secret scanning alerts that a live third-party API key was pushed to a private repository an hour ago. What should the team do first?

Rotate (revoke and replace) the affected credential immediately
Make the repository private to a smaller team
Dismiss the alert as "used in tests" so the dashboard is clean

Disable code scanning until the team has time for a full cleanup
Triage a baseline once, dismiss false positives with a reason, and gate pull requests only on new high-severity alerts while the backlog is burned down on a schedule
Enable every additional query suite so nothing is missed

Auto-merge every Dependabot pull request as soon as it opens
Remove the lockfile so installs always resolve the newest version

questions.scenario: A SaaS team allows password-only login. Their policy requires 8 or more characters with an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol, and a forced change every 90 days.
questions.stem: Which change brings the policy closest to NIST SP 800-63B-4?
options: Keep the composition rules, raise the minimum to 12, and extend rotation to 180 days.
Require at least 15 characters, remove the composition rules and scheduled rotation, and check new passwords against a breached-password blocklist.
Keep the current rules and add security questions as a backup check.
Require 64-character passwords and block paste so users must type them.

Hints and security questions SHALL NOT be used.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Pre-hash with plain SHA-512 and pass the hex digest to bcrypt.
Cap password length at 72 characters in the UI.
Raise the bcrypt work factor to 14.

Force every user to rotate their password weekly until the attack stops.

The data key encrypted (wrapped) by the KMS key, plus metadata such as IV and key id.

A WAF rule that blocks requests containing other tenants' ids.

questions.scenario: A product search endpoint uses the ORM's raw query method: the code builds "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + term + "%'" and passes the string in. A reviewer flags it; the author replies that the ORM protects them.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?

Move the query into a stored procedure that concatenates the term into dynamic SQL
Keep the raw query but pass the search term (with the % wildcards added to the value) as a bound parameter using the ORM's binding syntax
Add a web application firewall rule that blocks requests containing SQL keywords

A stored procedure that builds dynamic SQL from its input is still injectable.

Use unsafe-inline because static sites cannot use strict CSP
Use hash-based script-src entries for the two inline scripts
Allowlist the CDN hostname in script-src and leave the inline scripts as they are

Remove script-src and rely on default-src 'self'
Add unsafe-eval so dynamically loaded scripts are allowed

unsafe-eval enables eval-style code and does not solve script loading.

Set SameSite=None so the behaviour is consistent across browsers

questions.scenario: An API's CORS middleware copies the request's Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and always sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, "so any of our frontends work".
questions.stem: What is the impact and the fix?
options: No impact, because browsers block reflected origins
Any website can make credentialed requests and read the user's private responses; replace reflection with an exact-match allowlist of origins and send Vary: Origin
Only GET requests are affected; block GET requests
The fix is to send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials instead

The fix is a strict allowlist with exact matches, plus Vary: Origin when the header varies. Browsers reject the wildcard for credentialed requests, so that is not an option.
rationales: Browsers honour whatever the server sends; they cannot tell reflection from intent.

Send Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self') as a response header, optionally with X-Frame-Options for older browsers

Require the URL to start with https://
Only allow port 443 and keep following redirects

The library should be configured to use IPv6 only
Public IP checks are unnecessary if the domain is on an allowlist

rationales: Two lookups can both look public and the library's lookup can still differ.
Correct: pinning the connection to the checked IP removes the rebinding window.
IPv6 has its own internal ranges, including IPv4-mapped addresses.

Configure the instances to require IMDSv2 (session tokens) and disable IMDSv1
Change the metadata service to a different IP address

questions.stem: Which fix is best?
options: Replace ../ with an empty string in the file parameter
Use path.join instead of string concatenation
Look files up by a server-generated ID; if names must be used, resolve the canonical path and verify it starts with the upload directory plus a path separator
Return a generic 404 for missing files

The vulnerable code already uses path.join, which normalizes ../ rather than blocking it.

options: Blocklist dangerous extensions such as .php and .exe and keep everything else
Rename each file to a server-generated name and store it outside the web root (ideally on a separate server or storage service)
Allowlist permitted extensions and validate the file content instead of trusting the client's Content-Type
Keep the original filename and rely on client-side JavaScript to check file types

Base64-decode the cookie twice to make tampering harder
Catch exceptions from pickle.loads so malformed cookies are ignored
Encrypt the pickle with a key hardcoded in the source code

A data-only format with schema validation removes that class of bug. Encoding, error handling and hardcoded keys do not make untrusted pickles safe.

Encoding is not protection; the attacker can encode a payload the same way.
A malicious pickle runs its payload during loading, before any exception helps.
A key in source code can leak, and the format remains dangerous if it does.

Limit SVG uploads to 100 KB

The content is unchanged, and content sniffing or direct use can still treat it as SVG.

rationales: `*` allows the features in every frame, which is the opposite of the goal.
Referrer-Policy is unrelated to device features.
Correct: empty allowlists disable the features everywhere on the page.
This stops other sites from framing the page. It does not restrict the embedded widgets.

questions.scenario: A password-reset page has the reset token in its URL and loads analytics scripts and images from third-party domains. The team has not set a Referrer-Policy.
questions.stem: What is the most accurate assessment and fix?
options: The browser default sends only the origin cross-origin, but setting `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on this page removes any referrer leakage of the token.
Browsers send the full URL cross-origin by default, so the token always leaks unless you use `unsafe-url`.
Referrer-Policy has no effect on subresource requests, only on link clicks.
Use `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to stop the token being included.
questions.explanation: MDN states the default policy is now `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, which sends only the origin on cross-origin requests. Same-origin requests still carry the full URL, though, and older clients may behave differently, so `no-referrer` on a page with secrets in its URL is the defensive choice. Better still, avoid secrets in URLs.
rationales: Correct: the default limits cross-origin leakage, and no-referrer removes it.
The default is no longer full-URL. Also, `unsafe-url` is the policy that leaks the most.
Referrer-Policy applies to subresource and navigation requests alike.
nosniff controls MIME sniffing, not referrers.

questions.scenario: A load balancer accepts TLS 1.0 through 1.3 "for maximum compatibility". An audit flags it.
questions.stem: Which configuration aligns with current OWASP guidance?
options: Keep TLS 1.0 and 1.1 but restrict them to strong cipher suites.
Allow only TLS 1.2, because TLS 1.3 is not yet widely supported.
Keep all versions and add HSTS, which prevents downgrade.
Default to TLS 1.3, allow TLS 1.2 for compatibility, and disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
questions.explanation: The OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet says web applications must default to TLS 1.3 and may support TLS 1.2 for compatibility. It also says TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated by RFC 8996 and must be disabled. HSTS enforces HTTPS but does not choose protocol versions.
rationales: Strong ciphers do not make deprecated protocol versions acceptable.
TLS 1.3 is the recommended default, and dropping it is a regression.
HSTS forces HTTPS. It does not stop a client from negotiating an old TLS version.
Correct, matching the cheat sheet.

questions.scenario: Secret scanning alerts that a live production database password was committed to a public repository 40 minutes ago. The engineer on call proposes rewriting Git history first, then rotating the password over the weekend.
questions.stem: What should the team do first?
options: Rewrite history with a force-push, then rotate later once the change window opens.
Make the repository private, then decide whether rotation is needed.
Rotate the credential immediately and review access logs for its use since the commit. History rewriting is secondary.
Wait for the provider's partner program to revoke the secret automatically.
questions.explanation: GitHub's secret scanning guidance says to rotate the affected credential immediately, and notes that rewriting history is often unnecessary once the credential is revoked. A public secret can be copied within minutes, so the only thing that removes the attacker's access is invalidating it, followed by checking whether it was used.
rationales: The password stays valid during the delay and may already have been copied.
Hiding the repository does not invalidate copies that were already taken.
Correct: revoke or rotate first, then investigate use.
Partner revocation is the provider's choice and not guaranteed, and database passwords usually are not covered.

questions.scenario: An EU-based SaaS (the controller) confirms on Monday 09:00 that an attacker exfiltrated a customer table containing names and emails. The full scope will take a week to establish.
questions.stem: Which approach meets GDPR Article 33?
options: Wait until the investigation is complete, then notify within 72 hours of finishing it.
Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, giving information in phases as it becomes available.
Notify only the affected customers. Regulators are told only if more than 500 people are affected.
Notify within 4 business days of determining the breach is material.
questions.explanation: Article 33 requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware. Where details are not yet available, information may be provided in phases, and any delay must be explained. The four-business-days-after-materiality rule is the SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 deadline for US public companies, not GDPR.
rationales: The clock runs from awareness, not from the end of the investigation.
Correct: notify promptly, in phases if needed.
GDPR has no 500-person threshold, and telling individuals (Art. 34) is a separate duty.
That is the SEC 8-K Item 1.05 timing, which runs from the materiality determination.

questions.scenario: A two-week outage review is scheduled. A manager drafts the agenda item "identify who approved the bad deploy" and plans to include it in performance reviews.
questions.stem: According to Google SRE guidance, what is the better approach?
options: Run a blameless postmortem focused on contributing causes and systemic fixes, with owned action items, and share it openly.
Skip the postmortem, since the incident is resolved.
Hold the postmortem privately with management only, to avoid embarrassment.
Name the individual, but only in the internal version of the document.
questions.explanation: The SRE book says that, to be truly blameless, a postmortem must focus on identifying the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team. Blame discourages people from reporting problems. The book also describes sharing finished postmortems openly so others can learn, with action items tracked to completion.
rationales: Correct: blameless, cause-focused, action items, shared.
Skipping the postmortem loses the lessons and leaves the causes in place.
The SRE book favours transparent sharing over private reviews.
Naming someone in any version still turns the review into blame.

questions.scenario: A CI job that used a compromised third-party action had access to an npm automation token, an AWS deploy role via OIDC, and a Slack webhook. The malicious version ran for two days before the team pinned a clean SHA.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions belong in containment and eradication? (Select two.)
options: Revoke and reissue the npm token and the Slack webhook, and check npm for versions published during the window.
Review cloud audit logs for actions taken by the deploy role during the window, and tighten the role's trust policy if needed.
Delete the workflow run logs immediately so the leaked secrets are no longer visible.
Assume the OIDC-based AWS access is unaffected, because its credentials were short-lived, and take no action on AWS.
questions.explanation: CISA's guidance on both tj-actions and the npm worm is to treat secrets that the affected jobs could reach as exposed and rotate them. Containment also means checking what the attacker did with that access, such as packages published or cloud actions taken, because short-lived OIDC credentials could still have been used while valid. Logs are evidence, so preserve them rather than destroying them.
rationales: Correct: rotate exposed secrets and look for malicious publishes.
Correct: short-lived credentials could still be used while valid, so audit their use.
Destroying logs removes evidence. Rotation, not deletion, makes the leaked values useless.
Short-lived tokens were still usable by the malicious step while each job ran, so their use must be audited.
